stories.headline: US proposes tariffs of up to 25% on India; New Delhi rejects excess-capacity charge
stories.dek: The rate would fall to 17% if the two countries sign a trade deal, the US Trade Representative said after a Section 301 investigation.
stories.summary: The US Trade Representative proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods over alleged structural excess capacity, falling to 17% with a trade deal. India's commerce ministry said it has no such capacity in any sector and wants an early trade pact.
body: The United States on Wednesday proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods after a Section 301 investigation into alleged structural excess manufacturing capacity, with the rate to fall to 17% if India and the US sign a trade agreement.

India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said the same day that the notice from the US Trade Representative (USTR) was under examination. It said India has no structural excess capacity in any sector and had engaged constructively throughout the probe.

The ministry said India's position is that trade-related concerns should be addressed within the ongoing negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement. It said the government remains committed to working with the US towards an early conclusion of the pact, referring to the framework announced on February 2 and the joint statement of February 7.

The USTR examined 16 economies and made determinations against 14, including India, China, the European Union and Japan. It made no determination on Mexico or Norway. Hindustan Times reported that the 189-page India report cites Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat and the Production Linked Incentive scheme, and concludes that India's practices on manufacturing capacity are unreasonable and burden US commerce.

The USTR named pharmaceuticals and medical devices, steel, solar products and information and communications technology as sectors of particular concern. Hindustan Times reported that the proposed tariffs exempt generic medicines in dosage form, hundreds of drug ingredients and patented drugs.

At 17%, India's deal rate would be one percentage point below Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand at 18%, and three points below Vietnam and China at 20%, according to figures carried by PTI and Mathrubhumi. PTI reported that it was not immediately clear whether the one-point gap meets India's demand for an edge over Asian rivals.
USTR Jamieson Greer told CNBC the rates are "not really additive" and will generally not stack on existing duties. He said he did not expect any to take effect for "a couple of months".

Think tank GTRI said the dual-rate structure recreates the reciprocal-tariff regime under a new name and is meant to push partners into signing deals. Abhik Sengupta of the Helsinki Geoeconomics Society said India consumes most of what it produces and imports more than it exports.
Written comments are due by January 5, 2027, and hearings are scheduled to begin on January 25.
keyFacts: USTR proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods on Wednesday.
The rate would fall to 17% if India signs a trade deal with the US.
The probe covered 16 economies; determinations were made against 14.
Written comments are due January 5, 2027; hearings begin January 25.
India says it has no structural excess capacity in any sector.
stories.background: The USTR opened its excess-capacity investigation after the US Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. India and the US have negotiated a bilateral trade agreement since February 2025 and announced an interim framework in February 2026.
stories.whyItMatters: The proposal sets the tariff Indian exporters could face in the US market, depending on whether a trade deal is concluded before the measures take effect.

stories.headline: US proposes new tariffs of up to 20% on 14 trading partners, including China and EU
stories.dek: The EU says it "strongly" rejects the premise of the US overcapacity probe, while Beijing calls the charge a false issue; the duties face public comment first.
stories.summary: The US Trade Representative proposed new import duties on 14 economies, including China, the EU, Japan and India, after an eight-month probe into alleged excess production. The EU and China rejected the allegations, and US stocks fell on Wednesday.
body: The United States on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on imports from 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan and India, following an eight-month investigation into alleged excess industrial production.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), led by Jamieson Greer, ran the probe under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The proposed duties will go through a public comment period and a hearing before taking effect, possibly in January at the earliest, DW reported.

China would face an additional 20%, the joint-highest rate. DW reported that this would be added to roughly 25% in duties imposed during Donald Trump's first term, giving a combined 45% on some Chinese goods. About $30bn of Chinese imports being considered for tariff cuts would be exempt. BBC reported rates of up to 40% for China and up to 35% for Vietnam; the other outlets reported a 20% maximum.

A senior US official said the duties would respect the 15% cap agreed with the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and the 19% cap agreed with Malaysia. Greer told CNBC the proposals largely follow rates set under existing trade agreements, though some could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.

The other affected economies are Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. Mexico and Norway were part of the probe but are excluded because inquiries into them continue.

The USTR alleged that the economies are "promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles", according to a senior US official who spoke anonymously. In a separate announcement, it proposed a 10% duty on finished aircraft, which would affect Brazil's Embraer, and higher tariffs on Brazilian sugar.

European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill said: "We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity." The EU said it would study the findings and expects Washington to honour last year's trade agreement. Switzerland also rejected the allegations.

China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation." Beijing did not threaten retaliation, DW reported.

Gregory Shaffer, a Georgetown University Law Center professor, called the use of Section 301 "cynical". Capital Economics' Stephen Brown said the announcement was "not as alarming as it looks" because the duties largely replace earlier tariffs.

Al Jazeera reported that the Nasdaq fell 3.9% in early trading on Wednesday, the S&P 500 fell 2.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.4%. It noted that inflation data released the same day also affected markets.
A US-China trade truce is set to expire on January 10. Trump is due to host Xi Jinping at the G20 summit in Miami in December.
keyFacts: The US proposed tariffs of up to 20% on 14 economies on Wednesday.
China would face an additional 20%, with about $30bn of imports exempt.
Duties for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan would stay within a 15% cap.
Mexico and Norway are excluded while investigations continue.
The US-China trade truce expires on January 10.
stories.background: The Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February, ruling he lacked authority to impose them by declaring an economic emergency. The administration then launched Section 301 investigations, which allow tariffs against unfair trade practices.
stories.whyItMatters: Economists cited by the BBC and DW say tariffs can raise prices if businesses pass on costs; US consumer inflation was 3.7% in September. The outcome of the comment period will determine what exporters in the 14 economies face.

stories.headline: Houthis claim strikes on Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh tower as they near Aden
stories.dek: Saudi officials say air defences downed four drones at Ras Tanura and 11 people were hurt in Riyadh, while Houthi forces mass north of Aden.
stories.summary: The Houthis said they started fires at Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and hit Riyadh's financial district for a second time in a week. Saudi officials reported four drones downed and 11 injured, as Houthi forces closed to about 60 km of Aden.
body: Yemen's Houthi movement said on Wednesday it had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and a tower in Riyadh's financial district, while Saudi defence officials reported four drones shot down at the refinery and 11 people injured in the capital.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said "accurate and direct" strikes on Ras Tanura, which DW described as Saudi Arabia's largest refinery and a major crude export terminal, "caused fires to break out at the facility." DW reported a fire at the site. The Saudi account of damage there was limited to the drone interceptions.

Saree said the attack on the financial district was carried out "in three phases, with strikes hitting their targets accurately." Saudi officials said 11 people were injured when a tower there was hit. The Wall Street Journal identified the building as the Public Investment Fund Tower. It was also targeted on November 19, when no one was hurt.

On the ground, the Houthis have advanced to within about 60 kilometres of Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government, a military official said on Tuesday. The Guardian put the distance at about 50 miles (80km) and reported Houthi fighters massing north and east of the city, in areas around Kirish and al-Bayda.

The advance followed the withdrawal of government-allied forces from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait area on the western coast. Yemeni army spokesman Col. Majed al-Nuzaily said those forces are now on a defence line north and west of Aden. "Aden is a red line. It was a red line in 2015, when the Houthis came to the city and its people drove them out," he said.

Foreign ministry official Marwan al-Noman called on the United States and other Western countries to support the Yemeni coast guard in intercepting weapons smuggled to the Houthis. "The Houthis are a terrorist organisation," he said. The Houthis have not announced an intention to take Aden, the Guardian reported.

Saudi Arabia has carried out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to the independent Yemen Data Project. Houthi authorities allege Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July. Yemen's Interior Ministry said Houthi shelling in Taiz province killed three civilians, including a child, on Tuesday.
The Guardian reported that more than 350,000 people have been displaced since August and that international aid groups are drawing up contingency plans for a Houthi takeover of Aden.
keyFacts: Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed fires at Ras Tanura; Saudi officials said four drones were downed there.
Eleven people were injured when a Riyadh financial district tower was hit, Saudi officials said.
The same tower was targeted on November 19, with no injuries reported.
Houthi forces are about 60 km from Aden, a Yemeni military official said.
More than 350,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since August, the Guardian reported.
stories.background: The Houthis and Saudi-backed forces have fought for more than a decade in a civil war that is now 12 years old, by the Guardian's count. Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government since 2015. The Houthis swept aside government forces in September. DW links the conflict's wider significance to the ongoing conflict in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.whyItMatters: A Houthi capture of Aden would be a major setback for the Yemeni government and the Saudi-led coalition, the Guardian reported. Aid groups are preparing to cut or end operations in the city, and displacement and food insecurity are already severe.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu apologises to Supreme Court over Deepam lamp; Governor seeks explanation
stories.dek: The Madurai collector blamed the temple board for the lamp not being lit at the stone pillar, and the court said it will hear contempt petitions this week.
stories.summary: Madurai collector Nishant Krishna apologised to the Supreme Court on Wednesday for the Karthigai Deepam not being lit at the Thirupparankundram stone pillar, blaming the temple board. Governor Rajendra Arlekar has sought an explanation from the TVK government.
body: Madurai collector Nishant Krishna apologised to the Supreme Court on Wednesday for the failure to light the Karthigai Deepam at the stone pillar on Thirupparankundram hill, and said the temple's board of trustees had not authorised the team needed to do so.

"I sincerely apologise for the lamp not been lit at the Deepathoon," Krishna said in a status report to the court. He said he took "all the steps" between November 21 and 24 to secure the Devasthanam's authorisation, following the court's November 20 order.

According to the report, the board resolved on November 24 to light the lamp at the customary place, the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillayar temple. Krishna said the Devasthanam never communicated any authorisation of persons to light it at the pillar, and that he learnt of the board's decision only after the lamp was lit at 8.30 pm. He said he had emailed a reminder to the temple's executive officer at 3.47 pm.

Deccan Herald reported that the administration had planned a team of up to 10 authorised persons to perform the ritual between 6 pm and 6.30 pm, with nearly 5,800 security personnel and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS. The collector said there was no wilful disobedience on his part.

The temple board said it unanimously resolved to protect the temple's age-old customs. A statement signed by chairperson V Shanmugasundaram said such practices and Agama rules were "the unique religious identity of the temple". PTI reported that the temple priests, the Sthanikars, distanced themselves from the board's decision.

A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi declined to start contempt proceedings on its own. It said the registry will verify applications, including contempt petitions, and the court will see whether they can be listed on Thursday or Friday. A contempt petition was filed later on Wednesday, according to the court's website.
Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, for the state, called the outcome "unfortunate". Counsel for Hindu Dharma Parishad used the words "most unfortunate" and accused authorities of circumvention.

Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar has sought an explanation from the government, official sources told PTI. A letter asks for official information on the matter and on police instructions followed on the ground. South First reported, citing unnamed reports, that he invoked Article 167(b) of the Constitution.

BJP MP Sudhanshu Trivedi told a press conference in New Delhi that the government had neither followed nor implemented the court's judgement. He called it "another Shah Bano moment for the Congress" and accused the INDIA bloc of acting against Hindu sentiments. The Congress response was not part of the reporting reviewed here.

The court's November 20 order allowed the lighting at the pillar as a one-time measure with safeguards. It stayed the Madras High Court's findings on the pillar and said the arrangement creates no customary, religious or proprietary right.
keyFacts: The Supreme Court's November 20 order allowed a one-time lighting at the Deepathoon pillar.

stories.background: For decades the Karthigai Deepam has been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple on the lower slopes of Thirupparankundram hill. Hindu groups sought permission to light it at the Deepathoon, an ancient stone pillar higher up, about 50 metres from the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah. The dargah side has claimed ownership of the hilltop and opposed the move.
stories.whyItMatters: The court's handling of the contempt petitions could determine whether officials face action over the unfulfilled order, while the site dispute itself remains open for adjudication.

stories.headline: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker overturns and sets off fire on Cairo ring road
stories.dek: Egypt's health minister said the toll is preliminary and could rise, as prosecutors opened an investigation and began DNA tests to identify victims.
stories.summary: A fuel tanker overturned on Cairo's Ring Road on Wednesday evening and caught fire, killing at least 31 people and injuring 21, Egypt's health ministry said. The public prosecutor has opened an investigation.
body: A fuel tanker overturned on the Ring Road in Cairo's Warraq district on Wednesday evening and set off a fire that killed at least 31 people and injured 21 others, Egypt's health ministry said.

Early reports gave lower figures. Al Jazeera, the Associated Press and the South China Morning Post cited the ministry as saying at least 30 were dead, with 15 injured. The Public Prosecutor's office, quoted by The Hindu, put the injured at at least 25.

Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that the toll was preliminary and could rise. He said 39 ambulances were sent to the scene. The BBC reported that hospitals treated patients for burns and smoke inhalation.

Rescue workers were seen pulling people from burning cars, and Associated Press video showed firefighters tackling flames spreading among vehicles. The public prosecutor's office said more than two dozen cars and motorcycles were charred. DW, citing Egyptian authorities, put the number of burned vehicles at at least 27.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire started. State-owned media reported that the tanker overturned and doused nearby vehicles with petrol. Al-Ahram, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation, reported that the tanker belonged to a private contractor and that a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, causing the driver to lose control. It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the newspaper said. Those details have not been confirmed by officials.

The public prosecutor has opened an investigation and asked for DNA samples to be taken from the dead so that badly burned victims can be identified. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed condolences and directed the relevant authorities to support the families of the victims and the injured, according to DW.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Algeria's ambassador to Egypt also expressed condolences.

Unverified footage on social media showed flames and black smoke rising into the night sky. After the fire was put out, a large crowd gathered on the highway and emergency services blocked entry routes, the BBC reported.
keyFacts: At least 31 people were killed and 21 injured, according to Egypt's health ministry.
The crash happened on Ring Road in the Warraq district on Wednesday evening.
At least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, were burned, DW reported.
Thirty-nine ambulances were sent to the scene, the health minister said.
The public prosecutor has opened an investigation and ordered DNA tests on victims.
stories.background: The Ring Road encircles Greater Cairo. Road accidents kill thousands of people in Egypt every year, and speeding, poor roads and weak enforcement of traffic laws are cited as the main causes. In January, 21 people were killed and 16 injured in a multicar pileup near Beni Suef.
stories.whyItMatters: The toll could still rise, and families of victims await DNA identification of badly burned bodies. The investigation will examine how the tanker came to overturn.

stories.headline: Supreme Court declines interim bail to Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam for now
stories.dek: A bench led by CJI Surya Kant asked Delhi Police to respond by December 14 and sent the matter towards a three-judge bench on UAPA bail and delay.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to hear interim bail for Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, saying 'Not today', and issued notice to Delhi Police. It directed that a three-judge bench be constituted on UAPA bail and prolonged custody.
body: The Supreme Court on Wednesday declined to hear interim bail pleas from Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, issued notice to Delhi Police returnable on December 14, and directed that a three-judge bench be constituted for the matter.

The bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana asked the Registry to place the case before the CJI on the administrative side. It cited the court's May 22 order in Tasleem Ahmed v. State Government of NCT of Delhi, which referred to a larger bench the question of how delay in trial affects bail under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).

Senior advocates Kapil Sibal, for Khalid, and Siddhartha Dave, for Imam, pressed for interim relief, citing more than six years in custody. Sibal said only the legal question was under reference and the interim prayer should be heard separately. The bench replied: "Not today" and "We are aware of everything. We have done our homework and have gone through the January 5 judgment."

Reports differ on what happens to the interim prayer. PTI-based reports carried by Business Standard and ThePrint said the court would hear the police before considering it. The Hindu and Hindustan Times reported that the court declined to take up interim relief pending the larger bench's decision.

The CJI said he had to examine conflicting readings of the 2021 Najeeb ruling, which he authored. "I am being told what I have said," he remarked. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, for Delhi Police, noted that the May 22 reference arose from bail proceedings involving other accused in the same case.

Khalid and Imam are challenging a September 30 Delhi High Court ruling that rejected their fresh bail pleas. The High Court said it could not modify conditions set by the Supreme Court on January 5, when it denied them bail, saying their roles stood on a "qualitatively different footing". The Supreme Court allowed them to reapply after a year or once protected witnesses were examined, whichever came first.

In his petition, Imam said none of the more than 900 prosecution witnesses had been examined, 47 of them protected. He argued that his detention had become "punitive by reason of unreasonable and unjustified delay", and that the case was still at the stage of arguments on charge.

Five of the 18 accused, including Khalid and Imam, remain in custody. Delhi Police allege a larger conspiracy behind the violence in northeast Delhi in February 2020, which The Hindu reported left 53 people dead. Notice is returnable on December 14.

stories.background:

Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan said that ruling had not correctly applied the 2021 Najeeb judgment, which held that UAPA's bail bar could 'melt down' in cases of prolonged incarceration.

On May 22, Justices Aravind Kumar and P.B. Varale referred the question to the CJI for a larger bench and granted six months' interim bail to Tasleem Ahmed and Abdul Khalid Saifi.
stories.whyItMatters: Khalid and Imam stay in custody while the court sets up a larger bench, and its ruling on delay and UAPA bail could affect other accused held under the Act.

stories.headline: India says Hasina's voluntary return is separate from Dhaka's extradition request
stories.dek: Bangladesh has put 108 border guard platoons in seven districts ahead of the former prime minister's announced December 16 return, while India also raised attacks on minorities.
stories.summary: India's foreign ministry said Sheikh Hasina's voluntary return is a separate matter from Bangladesh's extradition request, and flagged attacks on minorities. Dhaka deployed 108 Border Guard Bangladesh platoons, 56 in Gopalganj, ahead of her planned December 16 return.
body: India's Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday that former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina's voluntary return to her country is a separate matter from Dhaka's request for her extradition, according to reports by The Wire and the Press Trust of India.

Asked about reports that Hasina would be handcuffed and taken into custody if she returned, the ministry said the issue is between the former prime minister and Dhaka, The Wire reported. PTI reported that India declined to comment on her plan to go back. The Wire said India also flagged attacks on minorities in Bangladesh. The full ministry statement was not available to Measured Edition.

Hasina's spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said on Tuesday that she would return on December 16, the day Bangladesh marks its 1971 victory over Pakistan. He said she had asked Dhaka to arrange her travel from New Delhi on the national carrier, Biman Bangladesh. Deccan Herald reported that her lawyer wrote to the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi on November 9 and 19 seeking travel documents.

Bangladeshi ministers responded sharply. Humaiun Kobir, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, said she could be brought back only "in handcuffs or under strict surveillance". Another minister, Shama Obaed Islam, said she would be arrested on arrival and treated under the same laws as any other convicted fugitive abroad.

On Wednesday, Border Guard Bangladesh said it had deployed 108 platoons in seven districts "to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and deal with any untoward situation", bdnews24.com reported. Of these, 56 are in Gopalganj, Hasina's home district. Another 18 are in Dhaka, 18 in Gazipur, six in Narayanganj, three in Chattogram, two in Mymensingh and one in Cox's Bazar. Four more platoons are on alert. A platoon has 30 to 40 personnel.

Police data cited by local media said 83 vehicles were set on fire and crude bombs were hurled at 87 locations between November 7 and 19. Police blamed Awami League activists and affiliated groups for several incidents. The party's activities are banned, and it is promoting a lockdown on November 29 and 30 through online platforms.

Hasina, 79, has lived in India since August 2024. A Dhaka tribunal sentenced her in absentia to death over the crackdown on protesters in 2024. She has denied wrongdoing and questioned the proceedings. India has acknowledged Dhaka's extradition requests but announced no decision, saying they are being examined through established processes.
Authorities have told police in 30 districts bordering India to step up surveillance and patrols with the BGB.

The BNP won the February 2026 election, from which the Awami League was barred.
stories.whyItMatters: The dispute affects India-Bangladesh relations and the security of Bangladeshi districts, particularly Gopalganj, where deployments and past arson attacks are concentrated.

stories.headline: India and China hold military commander talks in Arunachal sector, MEA says
stories.dek: The talks, led on the Indian side by Lt Gen Girish Kalia, followed reports of Chinese troop posturing near Upper Subansiri and were the second round since September.
stories.summary: Senior Indian and Chinese military commanders met in the Arunachal Pradesh sector in the second week of November to discuss border management and outstanding issues along the LAC, the external affairs ministry said on Wednesday. It was the second such round since September.
body: Senior military commanders of India and China held talks in the Arunachal Pradesh sector this month on improving border management and addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday.

Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, responding to a question at a regular briefing, said: "A meeting of the senior, highest military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently." He said such interactions are aimed at maintaining peace and tranquillity in border areas and preventing any escalation.
Jaiswal added that India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms.

Lt Gen Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army's 3 Corps, based near Dimapur in Nagaland, led the Indian side in the second week of November. The Chinese side was headed by his counterpart. The talks were believed to have lasted more than a week, according to Hindustan Times.

The Press Trust of India and Hindustan Times reported that the talks followed reports of aggressive posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC, especially in the Upper Subansiri region. In September, Kalia and a Chinese commander held flag talks in two sessions on either side of the LAC in the same sector.

Hindustan Times reported that the Indian Army and the People's Liberation Army had tensions at Taksing, in Upper Subansiri district, in July and August. India said at the time that both sides had agreed to use diplomatic and military mechanisms to "avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation".

The commander-level channel for the eastern and middle sectors came from the 24th round of Special Representatives talks in New Delhi on August 19, between National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi. That round produced 10 points of consensus. A similar mechanism already exists in the western sector, which includes Ladakh.

Asked separately about reports that Pakistan may have used Chinese satellite data to track Indian troop movements and military installations during Operation Sindoor, Jaiswal said: "We have seen some media reports on this particular issue." He said India would continue to follow developments that may bear on its security interests and take appropriate measures.
keyFacts: Talks were held in the second week of November in the Arunachal Pradesh sector.
Lt Gen Girish Kalia of 3 Corps led the Indian side.
They were the second round of such talks in the sector since September.
The 24th Special Representatives round on August 19 produced 10 points of consensus.
Nearly 50,000 Indian troops are deployed in eastern Ladakh, PTI reported.
stories.background: India and China began rebuilding ties after a military standoff in eastern Ladakh that followed the 2020 Galwan Valley clashes. In October 2024 the two sides reached a disengagement understanding covering Depsang and Demchok, the last friction points there. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has since met President Xi Jinping in Kazan, Tianjin and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September.
stories.whyItMatters: The talks use a new commander-level mechanism for the eastern sector, where reported friction has occurred this year. India says the state of the border will determine the course of the wider relationship.

stories.headline: Israeli judges urge prosecutors to reconsider Netanyahu bribery case
stories.dek: The Jerusalem panel told the attorney general the chance of conviction in Case 4000 is low, as Gadi Eisenkot works to form a government by December 6.
stories.summary: Judges in Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial told the attorney general on Wednesday that a conviction in the most serious of three cases is unlikely. Netanyahu called for the trial to end immediately; his rival Gadi Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government.
body: Judges in Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial told Israel's attorney general on Wednesday that the chance of conviction in the bribery case against the caretaker prime minister is low, and recommended that prosecutors reconsider it.

The Jerusalem District Court panel summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to the hearing, a step the BBC described as highly unusual. "The chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, according to Israeli media reports cited by the BBC. Al Jazeera, also citing Israeli media, reported the judge said proving bribery in the case faced "considerable difficulties".

The case, known as Case 4000, is considered the most serious Netanyahu faces. Prosecutors allege he offered regulatory favours to the telecoms company Bezeq in exchange for positive coverage on the Walla news site, after negotiating with its controlling shareholder, Shaul Elovitch. Netanyahu is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust. Both men deny wrongdoing.

On the other two cases, the judges questioned whether Netanyahu's alleged conduct in Case 2000 met the threshold for a crime and recommended reconsidering it. That case concerns an alleged deal with the owner of Yediot Aharonot for favourable coverage in exchange for curbs on the rival Israel Hayom. In Case 1000, which involves alleged gifts of luxury items, the judges left open the possibility of conviction and suggested resolving it through an agreement, Israeli media reported.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal, Al Jazeera reported.

In a televised statement at the Knesset, Netanyahu said the "fabricated cases" against him were falling apart. "The trial must end immediately," he said. "Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son."

Defence Minister Israel Katz, a member of the caretaker government, wrote on X that "the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset". Netanyahu's right-wing allies broadly demanded the trial be ended, France 24 reported.

The ruling comes during coalition talks after inconclusive elections on October 27. Netanyahu's bloc won more seats than Eisenkot's, but neither secured a majority, and President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.

Eisenkot's Yashar party agreed on Tuesday to sign a coalition pact with Avigdor Liberman's Israel Our Home party. Liberman said Eisenkot was on track, according to The New York Times. The left-wing Democrats suspended coalition talks on Tuesday; Liberman has ruled out a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot has a 28-day mandate ending December 6 and could request a 14-day extension. If he fails, Netanyahu would get a chance to form a government. If nobody succeeds, another election would be held next year.
keyFacts: Judges said chances of conviction in Case 4000 are low, according to Israeli media.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said she would consider the recommendations.
Netanyahu's trial opened in May 2020; he denies all charges.

Elections on October 27 produced no outright majority for either bloc.
stories.background: Netanyahu was first charged in 2019 and is the first sitting Israeli prime minister to face a criminal trial. Proceedings were prolonged in part by the Gaza war, and judges reduced the number of hearings for security reasons. He remains subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over the Gaza war, which he denies.
stories.whyItMatters: Al Jazeera reported that if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence, so the trial's outcome is tied to the coalition talks.

perspectives.summary: Netanyahu says the cases are fabricated and politically motivated and are collapsing, and that the trial must end immediately. Katz called the trial flawed from the outset.

perspectives.summary: Netanyahu's opponents argue that his fear of prison has distorted his decision-making and made him dependent on far-right coalition partners. Eisenkot's camp says it is making progress towards forming a government.

stories.headline: Sensex gains 1,502 points as rupee reaches eight-month high
stories.dek: Foreign fund inflows and Brent crude below $90 a barrel supported buying in large-cap stocks, with the Nifty up 1.85% on Wednesday.
stories.summary: The Sensex rose 1,502 points to 83,938 and the Nifty gained 470 points to 25,819 on Wednesday. The rupee climbed 62 paise to 92.23 against the dollar, its highest in eight months.
body: The benchmark Sensex rose 1,502 points, or 1.82%, to 83,938 on Wednesday, while the Nifty gained 470 points, or 1.85%, to 25,819, as foreign fund inflows and softer crude oil prices lifted large-cap stocks.

Earlier in the session the Sensex had jumped 2,062.22 points to a day's high of 84,498.21, and the Nifty touched 25,951.65. Both indices had fallen sharply on Monday, when the Sensex lost 1,483.72 points, or 1.77%, to settle at 82,435.99. Markets were shut on Tuesday for Prakash Gurpurb of Sri Guru Nanak Dev.
Investors' wealth rose by ₹3.49 lakh crore to ₹5,12,48,042.08 crore on the day, The Hindu reported.

Among Sensex stocks, Hindustan Unilever rose 5.94%, Trent 3.59%, ICICI Bank 3.44%, IndiGo 3.24%, HDFC Bank 3.18% and Bajaj Finance 3.04%. FMCG, pharma, financial services, banking and auto were the main sectoral gainers. Metal and media lagged. The Nifty Midcap 100 rose 0.30%, while the Nifty Smallcap 100 fell 0.44%.

Brent crude traded 1.43% lower at $90.10 per barrel in morning trade, and analysts said it later eased below $90. Foreign institutional investors bought equities worth ₹5,672.99 crore on Monday, according to exchange data.

The rupee gained 62 paise to 92.23 against the dollar in interbank trade, from an overnight close of 92.85. It touched 92.1850 during the day. Kunal Sodhani, head of treasury at Shinhan Bank, attributed the rise to strong foreign portfolio inflows, softer crude, better domestic dollar supply and exporter dollar selling.

The two analysts quoted gave different figures for November's foreign inflows. V K Vijayakumar of Geojit Investments put them at a record $13.2 billion so far this month. Sodhani said they stood at $14 billion.

Asian markets were weak on Wednesday. South Korea's Kospi fell 6.16% and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.78%. Vijayakumar said swings in AI-linked trades were driving volatility in global equities, and called the Indian market resilient.

Shrikant Chouhan of Kotak Neo said some consolidation should not be a surprise after the speed of the recent rally. He expects the Nifty to trade broadly in a 25,000–26,000 range in the very short term. Sodhani said the rupee could test 91.50–92.00 if conditions persist, though RBI dollar purchases could limit gains.
keyFacts: Sensex rose 1,502 points, or 1.82%, to 83,938 on Wednesday.
Nifty gained 470 points, or 1.85%, to 25,819.
Rupee rose 62 paise to 92.23 against the dollar, an eight-month high.
Investors' wealth increased by ₹3.49 lakh crore on the day.
Brent crude traded below $90 a barrel.
stories.background: The Sensex fell 1,483.72 points on Monday, November 23, and markets were closed on Tuesday for a holiday. Wednesday's gains followed that fall.
stories.whyItMatters: Analysts said lower oil prices and a firmer rupee ease import costs and inflation expectations, which could help fuel-consuming sectors such as aviation, auto and paints.

stories.headline: MEA says Saurav Das was told to clarify birthplace and not use passport
stories.dek: The Delhi High Court is due to hear the CJP co-convenor's plea on Thursday, after Das alleged that BJP-aligned accounts leaked his passport details.
stories.summary: The Ministry of External Affairs said the Chennai passport office asked CJP co-convenor Saurav Das to clarify his place of birth within seven days and not to use his passport meanwhile. Das, stopped at Delhi airport on his way to London, will argue his plea on Thursday.
body: The Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday that the Regional Passport Office in Chennai issued Cockroach Janta Party co-convenor Saurav Das a show-cause notice on November 23 seeking clarification of his place of birth within seven days, and advised him not to use his passport until he replied.

Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the notice was based on "reports we received from the relevant law enforcement authorities". He told the ministry's bi-weekly briefing that the passport application requires correct information, and that a notice is issued when a discrepancy, which amounts to suppression of facts, is noted or reported by authorities.

Das was stopped at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport in the early hours of November 24 as he prepared to board a flight to London. The Hindu reported that his passport was issued in 2019 and that the notice was emailed at 7:30 pm on Monday, hours before the 1 am flight. Das has said he received it "just five hours before my flight" and that its sole purpose was to harass him. He said he was shown no order or Look Out Circular.

Das said he was travelling to speak about the 'Cockroach movement' at Oxford, Cambridge, the London School of Economics and Edinburgh. News18 reported that the Oxford Union event is on December 1. It also reported, citing several reports, that his passport lists Chennai as his place of birth, which it described as incorrect. The MEA did not state what the discrepancy is.

Das moved the Delhi High Court. The matter was mentioned on Wednesday before Acting Chief Justice Nitin Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma, who did not grant an urgent hearing, according to Outlook. The plea, filed through advocate Krishnaraj Bapat, will be argued by senior advocate Akhil Sibal on Thursday.

On Wednesday Das also wrote on X that "certain BJP-aligned social media handles have now leaked my passport" and asked whether the MEA would clarify if such leaks were routine. He said he would file criminal complaints against every handle involved. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said the passport had been leaked "from within the system". The ministry's briefing, as reported, did not address the allegation.
Separately, the Madras High Court issued notice on October 30 on a petition seeking an investigation into Das's identity and nationality, among other issues, Outlook reported.

The notice was emailed at 7:30 pm, before a 1 am flight to London, according to The Hindu.
Das's passport was issued by the Chennai passport office in 2019.
The Delhi High Court will hear his plea on Thursday; Akhil Sibal will argue it.
The Madras High Court issued notice on October 30 on a petition about Das's identity and nationality.
stories.background: Das is co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta Party. He said he was invited to speak at four UK universities. The Madras High Court petition on his identity and nationality predates the passport notice, according to Outlook.
stories.whyItMatters: The Delhi High Court's hearing will determine whether Das can travel to the UK for the planned lectures, including the Oxford Union event on December 1.

stories.headline: Meta executives meet Congress leaders in Delhi over content moderation bias claims
stories.dek: Congress raised restrictions on its leaders' accounts and alleged favouritism towards the BJP; Meta made no commitments and said it follows local law and is neutral.
stories.summary: Meta's top India executives held closed-door talks with Congress on Tuesday, the company's first direct engagement since Youth Congress protests began. Meta made no commitments, saying it is bound by local laws and neutral towards all parties.
body: Meta's top executives in India met Congress leaders in Delhi on Tuesday to try to defuse protests over the company's content moderation, according to four people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters.

Aman Jain and Natasha Jog represented Meta at the meeting at Congress headquarters, one person said. The Hindu, citing Congress sources, reported that Supriya Shrinate, who heads the party's social media department, attended, and that the meeting took place at Meta's request. Neither side has commented officially.
The talks lasted more than 40 minutes, Reuters reported. It was Meta's first direct engagement with the party since the Youth Congress began protesting on Friday.

The Youth Congress has demanded that Meta restore accounts taken down on government orders and explain how its algorithms restrict posts. Its members have clashed with police near Meta offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram.

Meta's executives raised concerns about the protests at its offices and about posters depicting chief executive Mark Zuckerberg, the sources said. Congress raised a rise in restrictions on its leaders' accounts and posts, and allegations that Meta favours the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Meta has denied favouritism.

According to the sources, Meta said some removals followed its policy on AI-generated content. Congress cited BJP posts also made with AI that had not been taken down, and said the takedown policy appeared arbitrary. The Hindu's sources said Ms Shrinate argued that AI-generated BJP content targeting Congress leaders remained online.

She also said the protests followed the blocking of the Instagram handles of Youth Congress chief Uday Bhanu Chhib and of Manish Sharma, the All India Congress Committee in-charge for the Youth Congress. Youth Congress sources said the handles have since been restored.

Meta made no commitments, explained that it was bound by local laws and stressed that it was neutral towards all political parties, the sources said. The company told Reuters it moderates content in India in accordance with the law. Congress did not respond to Reuters' request for comment.
BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari wrote on X on Saturday: "This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of private companies."
Posters and banners showing Zuckerberg in the uniform of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh have appeared in Delhi, Kolkata, Patna, Mumbai and Bengaluru, Reuters reported.
keyFacts: Meeting held on Tuesday, November 24, at Congress headquarters in Delhi.
Meta was represented by Aman Jain and Natasha Jog; Supriya Shrinate attended for Congress, per The Hindu.
Talks lasted more than 40 minutes, according to Reuters.

Youth Congress protests began on Friday in several cities.
stories.background: Meta's company disclosures show it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts under local laws in India in the first half of 2026, against about 70,000 in all of 2025. Meta attributes the rise to India's amended IT rules, which require faster and more proactive takedowns. The increase has fed a debate over free speech as the government steps up removal demands.
stories.whyItMatters: India is Meta's biggest market by users, and the company faces government takedown demands on one side and opposition accusations of bias on the other.

stories.headline: Adityanath says SP-Congress alliance has failed as seat-sharing talks stall in UP
stories.dek: The Samajwadi Party has offered the Congress 26 of 403 seats; Congress leaders, who had sought many more, called the manner of the offer disrespectful.
stories.summary: Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said the SP-Congress alliance had failed before the polls, after the SP announced candidates for five seats while talks continued. The Congress is reported to want 100 to 120 seats against the SP's offer of 26.
body: Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said in Lucknow on Wednesday that the Samajwadi Party-Congress alliance had "failed even before the elections", after the SP named candidates for five Assembly seats while seat-sharing talks with the Congress were still under way.

"What could be a greater humiliation. On one side, meetings are being held between the two parties over seat-sharing, while on the other, candidates are being announced," Adityanath said at a media summit, according to The Hindu.

SP leader Ram Gopal Yadav said on Tuesday that the party had offered the Congress 26 of the 403 seats. The SP announced candidates for Saharanpur, Kairana, Amroha, Lalitpur and Behat, PTI reported. NDTV, citing sources, reported that Behat and Saharanpur are also on the Congress wishlist.

The Congress is understood to have first sought 181 seats, then cut its demand. India Today reported that it submitted a revised list of about 100 to 120 constituencies on Monday. NDTV put the earlier reductions at 131 and then 110.

SP president Akhilesh Yadav on Tuesday asked the Congress to identify more seats beyond the 26 offered. He said the parties should look at an "equation for victory rather than seats" and that the SP might point out winnable seats the Congress had not considered. "This is not about seats, but about victory," he said.

Congress MP and Uttar Pradesh working president Imran Masood rejected that approach. "We are not beggars that you will give us whatever you want," he told NDTV, and said the SP had sent its list of 26 seats through the media. He added: "We don't need instructions from Akhilesh ji."

SP MP Iqra Hasan called Masood's remarks "irresponsible" and "derogatory" and said any alliance was bigger than "any one individual's aspirations or ego". Another SP MP, Zia Ur Rahman Barq, told PTI the matter was, for the time being, "personal" and that the party had received no such message from the Congress.
NDTV reported that sources close to Masood said the Congress was planning to contest against the SP at least in Saharanpur.

Separately, Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya told reporters in Jaunpur that only the lotus is the BJP's face in elections and that elected MLAs would choose their leader after the polls. He said he could not decide whether the next chief minister would be Adityanath or someone else.
Adityanath later told a private TV channel: "Everyone knows who the CM face is and who is not." He said every party candidate, himself included, would contest on the lotus symbol.
Leaders of both opposition parties indicated that another round of talks would be held within days, NDTV reported. The UP polls are expected early next year.
keyFacts: SP has offered the Congress 26 of 403 Assembly seats, Ram Gopal Yadav said on Tuesday.
The Congress reportedly submitted a list of about 100 to 120 seats on Monday.

stories.background: The SP and Congress contested the 2017 Assembly polls together and the 2022 polls separately. In 2022 the BJP won 255 seats and the SP 111; the Congress won two. They revived the alliance for the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, when the SP gave the Congress 17 of 80 seats; the Congress won six and the SP 37.
stories.whyItMatters: The seat split will determine how the two main opposition parties in Uttar Pradesh contest the state's Assembly elections, expected early next year.

stories.headline: Ukraine says it hit five Russian aircraft at Savasleyka airfield and two Samara refineries
stories.dek: Separately, reports based on hacked Russian statistics data put Russian military deaths between 470,000 and 700,000; the Kremlin declined to comment on the figures.
stories.summary: Ukraine's General Staff said it damaged three MiG-31 and two Su-34 aircraft at Russia's Savasleyka airfield, and Kyiv said it hit refineries in Samara. Separately, media reports on hacked data put Russian war deaths at up to 700,000.
body: Ukraine said on Wednesday it damaged five Russian military aircraft at the Savasleyka airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region, about 300km east of Moscow, and also struck two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region.

Kyiv's General Staff said three MiG-31 and two Su-34 aircraft were hit. It said the extent of the damage was still being assessed and that "there may be even better news to come". It did not say what weapons were used. Russia has not commented on the airfield strike, according to the BBC.
Savasleyka hosts aircraft Russia uses to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs. Take-offs by MiG-31s, which carry Kinzhal missiles, often trigger nationwide alerts in Ukraine.

In Samara, regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said air defences downed 145 drones overnight. He said one person was killed and several towns lost power. Reuters reported that Syzran and Samara, both on the Volga, host three major refineries, and that unverified social media reports said the Syzran and Kuibyshev refineries were attacked. Reuters said it could not verify that.
Ukraine's defence ministry said: "Did you repair them? We'll hit them again." Kyiv also said it hit a radar system and fuel and logistics depots in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for tighter security at energy facilities. He said Russia had stabilised its domestic fuel market without "critical damage" and that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate. Ukrainian refinery strikes eased after US President Donald Trump's mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire but have picked up sharply since the end of last month, Reuters reported.

Ukraine also remains under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between November 24 and 25, the BBC reported, and thousands are without power after strikes on energy infrastructure.

Separately, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday declined to comment on reports that 470,000 to 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed. "The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the defence ministry of the Russian Federation," he said, adding: "I suggest not to pay attention to any other data."

The reports draw on records from Russia's statistics agency, Rosstat, which the Belarusian Cyberpartisans and a pro-Ukrainian group, Silent Crow, said they obtained by hacking and published earlier this month. Several international outlets said the data showed close to 500,000 confirmed deaths. Meduza and Mediazona, banned independent Russian outlets, said the toll could reach 700,000 if soldiers listed as "missing" are counted.
keyFacts: Ukraine says three MiG-31s and two Su-34s were hit at Savasleyka airfield.

stories.background: Russia has not published an official military death toll since September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had died in the first six months, a figure widely seen as an undercount. In July, the US-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies put Russian deaths at about 450,000 and Ukrainian deaths at 125,000-150,000. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said in February that around 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers had been killed.
stories.whyItMatters: Ukraine's strikes target Russian oil processing and air capacity, and the leaked-data estimates offer the most detailed outside picture yet of Russian losses, which Moscow does not disclose.

stories.headline: Cabinet approves ₹11,000-crore construction equipment scheme, Silchar airport
stories.dek: The Union Cabinet also cleared a second container terminal at Kamarajar Port in Tamil Nadu, estimated at ₹4,288.26 crore under a public-private partnership model.
stories.summary: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved an eight-year, ₹11,000-crore incentive scheme for construction and infrastructure equipment manufacturing. It also cleared a ₹2,014-crore greenfield airport at Doloo in Silchar and a second container terminal at Kamarajar Port.
body: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved a ₹11,000-crore scheme to promote domestic manufacturing of construction and infrastructure equipment (CIE), along with a new airport at Silchar in Assam and a second container terminal at Kamarajar Port in Tamil Nadu.

The equipment scheme will run for eight years from FY 2026-27 and be implemented by the Ministry of Heavy Industries, according to Business Standard. Deccan Herald reported that the government aims to attract ₹21,000 crore in investment under it.

It has two components. The first is a sales-linked incentive for eligible original equipment manufacturers and component makers, at graded rates of 13 per cent to 8 per cent of incremental sales over five years. The second is a grant of up to ₹375 crore, in the nature of viability gap funding, for a dedicated CIE testing facility.

The scheme targets equipment such as ship-to-shore cranes, tunnel boring machines, hydraulic excavators and off-highway trucks. Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, briefing the media, said: "This scheme will help us achieve Atmanirbharta in the field."
Deccan Herald reported that India's CIE industry was worth ₹97,500 crore in FY 2024-25, with nearly half of it imported, mostly from China.

The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved a greenfield airport at Doloo in Assam's Cachar district at an estimated ₹2,014 crore, to be funded by the Airports Authority of India from its own resources. The existing Silchar airport is a civil enclave of about 70 acres on an Indian Air Force and AAI site. An official release said Doloo will ease its operational and space constraints.

The airport will have a 12,351-square-metre terminal able to handle 800 passengers at peak hours and 1.01 million passengers a year. It will have a 2,705-metre runway suitable for A-320 aircraft, and an apron for six A-320s plus an isolation bay.

The Cabinet also cleared a second container terminal at Kamarajar Port on a design, build, finance, operate and transfer basis, at an estimated ₹4,288.26 crore including GST. Phase I is put at ₹2,429.32 crore and Phase II at ₹1,858.94 crore. Kamarajar Port Ltd will separately bear an estimated ₹450 crore for dredging.

The 900-metre terminal, with an 18-metre design draft, is planned to handle 2 million TEUs a year and vessels of up to 24,346 TEUs. The existing terminal has a capacity of 0.8 million TEUs and handled about 0.7 million in FY 2025-26, utilisation of about 88 per cent, the statement said.
keyFacts: The CIE manufacturing scheme has an outlay of ₹11,000 crore over eight years from FY 2026-27.
Incentives range from 13 per cent to 8 per cent of incremental sales; testing grant up to ₹375 crore.
Silchar's Doloo airport is estimated at ₹2,014 crore, with a 2,705-metre runway.
Kamarajar Port's second container terminal is estimated at ₹4,288.26 crore and 2 million TEUs capacity.
stories.background: Kamarajar Port Ltd handled 49.08 million tonnes of cargo and 1,008 vessels in FY 2025-26, including more than 7 lakh TEUs of container traffic, according to the official statement cited by News18.
stories.whyItMatters: The equipment scheme aims to cut reliance on imported machinery, nearly half of the domestic market. The port terminal would add container capacity as the existing terminal runs at about 88 per cent utilisation.

stories.headline: RBI Bulletin says economy resilient, oil pass-through limited, food price pressure broad
stories.dek: Retail inflation rose to 6.09 per cent in October, above the monetary policy committee's tolerance band, with food prices the main driver, the central bank's monthly publication said.
stories.summary: The RBI's November Bulletin said India's economy stayed resilient in October on credit demand and exports, and that the oil price shock has fed through to retail fuel prices only to a limited degree. Food prices, however, remain under broad-based pressure.
body: The Reserve Bank of India said in its November Bulletin, released on Wednesday, that the Indian economy remained resilient in October, while pressure on food prices stayed broad-based and headline retail inflation rose to 6.09 per cent.

Consumer price inflation climbed from 5.54 per cent in September, according to Business Standard's account of the Bulletin. The October reading is above the upper tolerance level of 6 per cent set for the monetary policy committee. The Hindu noted that the level was last seen in October 2024.

The State of the Economy article said high-frequency data up to November 19 pointed to continued pressure on food prices. Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up, and edible oil prices rose across the board, led by mustard oil. Vegetables showed a mixed picture: onion prices rose moderately, tomato prices fell sharply and potato prices increased.

Pressure was not limited to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions recording sequential increases in October. Inflation rose in both rural and urban areas, with food and beverages inflation above 6 per cent in each. Most states and Union Territories stayed in the 4-6 per cent range, but more of them reported rates above 6 per cent.

On activity, the RBI said high-frequency indicators showed resilience, underpinned by strong bank and non-bank credit growth and sustained double-digit export growth. Bank credit grew 19.5 per cent year-on-year at the end of October, while deposits grew nearly 17 per cent. The trade deficit narrowed from a year earlier.

Gross GST collections in October were the second-highest monthly level since the tax was introduced in July 2017, the Bulletin said. Listed private non-financial companies reported stronger sales growth in the September quarter of FY27, led by manufacturing.

A separate article on imported inflation found that the West Asia conflict produced a sharper crude oil price shock than the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Pass-through to retail fuel prices has been relatively lower this time, limiting pressure on imported inflation. Imported items make up 8.5 per cent of the new CPI basket (base 2024=100) but contributed around 18 per cent of headline inflation in October 2026.
The Indian basket of crude oil averaged $95 per barrel during November 1-18, below its October peaks. The Hindu reported that the absence of a durable peace in West Asia kept markets volatile.

Business Standard reported that overseas investors put nearly $14 billion into Indian equities so far in November. The Bulletin said net inflows through external commercial borrowings and NRI deposits also remained strong.
The Bulletin states that the views in its articles are those of the authors and not of the Reserve Bank.
keyFacts: CPI inflation was 6.09 per cent in October, up from 5.54 per cent in September.
Bank credit grew 19.5 per cent year-on-year at end-October; deposits grew nearly 17 per cent.
Imported items are 8.5 per cent of the CPI basket but contributed about 18 per cent of October inflation.
The Indian crude basket averaged $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
11 of the 12 CPI divisions recorded sequential increases in October.
stories.background: The RBI's monthly Bulletin carries the central bank's State of the Economy assessment along with research articles. The November issue also included studies on NBFC performance in 2025-26 and on the effect of US monetary policy on Indian markets.
stories.whyItMatters: Inflation above the monetary policy committee's tolerance band affects household food and fuel costs, while the Bulletin's finding of limited fuel pass-through points to how far the crude shock has reached consumers.

stories.headline: Supreme Court sets aside stay on Vinay Kulkarni's life sentence, orders surrender
stories.dek: A bench of Justices Mishra and Chandrashekhar called the Karnataka High Court's July 31 order perverse and cancelled the bail bonds of the eight convicts.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday set aside the Karnataka High Court's stay of former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni's conviction and life sentence in the 2016 murder of BJP leader Yogesh Gowda. Kulkarni and the other convicts must surrender within two weeks.
body: The Supreme Court on Wednesday set aside a Karnataka High Court order that had stayed the conviction and suspended the life sentence of former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni in the 2016 murder of BJP leader Yogesh Gowda, and directed him to surrender within two weeks.

A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar cancelled the bail bonds of Kulkarni and other convicts and ordered them to surrender before the concerned court. Hindustan Times reported that eight convicts were covered by the order; South First said the court's direction applied to Kulkarni and the other convicted accused.

The bench described the High Court's July 31 order as "perverse". It said the High Court had proceeded on a "misconception" that Kulkarni would stand disqualified as a member of the legislative assembly if the conviction were upheld.

"If that is how the power of the court to stay the judgement of conviction is to be interpreted then every convicted legislator would automatically become entitled to an order staying the conviction," the bench said. It held that disqualification under Section 8(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 is a statutory consequence that cannot be avoided by showing an arguable case.

The court said a stay of conviction needs a higher threshold than a good prima facie case: a "palpable mistake" in the judgement that makes it illegal. Deccan Herald reported that the bench also faulted the High Court for relying on the statement of the deceased's wife, who had been declared hostile, to assess motive.

On suspension of sentence, the court rejected the idea that long pendency of an appeal is enough. "It is a wrong notion that pendency of the criminal appeal and its remote possibility of hearing in near future can be a ground to suspend the sentence in grave offences like murder, dacoity, rape, ransom etc.," it said. The bench added that the High Court had given no reason why those convicted on April 15 should be treated differently.

The court was hearing appeals filed by the Karnataka government, the Central Bureau of Investigation and Gowda's family. South First reported that the ruling does not dispose of the appeals against the convictions, which the High Court will continue to hear. Deccan Herald reported that Kulkarni stands disqualified as an MLA; South First said he was disqualified with effect from May 2 after his conviction.

Gowda, a Dharwad Zilla Panchayat member, was attacked at his gym in Saptapur, Dharwad, on June 15, 2016. The CBI described Kulkarni as the main conspirator. The convicts must now surrender within two weeks of Wednesday's order.
keyFacts: The Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, and ordered surrender within two weeks.
The High Court's July 31 order stayed Kulkarni's conviction and suspended his life sentence.
Yogesh Gowda was killed at his gym in Saptapur, Dharwad, on June 15, 2016.
The trial court convicted Kulkarni on April 15; sentencing followed two days later, South First reported.
The High Court will continue hearing the appeals against the convictions.
stories.background:
The case was first investigated by Dharwad police and moved to the CBI in 2019. South First reported that the CBI arrested Kulkarni in November 2020. He got Supreme Court bail in August 2021, which the court cancelled in June 2025 after finding material indicating he tried to influence prosecution witnesses.

The CBI's case, as reported by South First, was that Gowda had refused to withdraw from the 2016 Zilla Panchayat election, leading to enmity with Kulkarni. Kulkarni won the Dharwad seat in 2023 by 18,114 votes.
stories.whyItMatters: The ruling returns Kulkarni and the other convicts to custody while their appeals are pending, and sets out the test courts must apply before staying a legislator's conviction.

stories.headline: Supreme Court tells trial court to defer Senthil Balaji cash-for-jobs proceedings
stories.dek: A bench led by the Chief Justice said prosecution should not shift with the government in power, as it listed the matter for hearing on December 11.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court directed a trial court to adjourn the cash-for-jobs case against former Tamil Nadu minister V Senthil Balaji to the week of December 14. The bench said the conduct of prosecution should not change with the political executive.
body: The Supreme Court directed a trial court to adjourn the cash-for-jobs case against former Tamil Nadu minister V Senthil Balaji to a date in the week beginning December 14, and remarked that prosecution should not change with the government in power.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana passed the direction after senior advocate Kapil Sibal, for Balaji, said the case was listed before the trial court for framing of charges. The state denied that the matter was listed for that purpose. Sibal said trial court hearings were due on November 26 and 28.

Sibal first asked for an early Supreme Court hearing on Friday. Tamil Nadu Additional Advocate General Haripriya Padmanabhan said she had difficulty with that day. The state suggested December 11, and the bench posted the matter for that date.

Sibal told the court: "I don't want charge to be framed and then come to your lordships. Either he defers that, or the matter is heard earlier. They can't have it both ways." The Chief Justice said the court was only on the issue of bail, so the trial court could defer proceedings.

Senior advocate Rajiv Shakdher, for the state, said the Supreme Court was concerned with one case and the clubbing of chargesheets in it, CC 24/2021. Sibal said the respondents also wanted other complaint cases clubbed. Deccan Herald reported that Shakdher said applications in three of the cases concerned discharge and framing of charges.

The Chief Justice said the allegations against Balaji might be serious but that he should not be condemned unheard. Justice Bagchi noted that the cases were registered in 2021 and 2022 and were being heard in 2026. "Heavens won't fall," he said.

When the state argued that the trial had progressed after the government changed, Justice Bagchi said: "We are not bothered [about that]. That is the worst part of the administration of criminal justice - that the texture of prosecution changes with the texture of political executive. One government drags its feet, another goes post-haste."

Shakdher asked the bench not to record the observations in its order and said appropriate instructions would be issued. The bench said it was not making a formal observation but expected the prosecution to act with fairness and reasonableness.

Justice Bagchi said the order would help the state, as the trial court might otherwise have fixed the matter in January. Shakdher said day-to-day trial was under way in the case. Justice Bagchi replied that "this day to day trial is a myth".
The Supreme Court will next hear the matter on December 11.
keyFacts: The trial court must adjourn the case to a date in the week commencing December 14.
The bench comprised CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
The Supreme Court will next hear the matter on December 11.
The criminal cases against Balaji were registered in 2021 and 2022.
Kapil Sibal appeared for Balaji; Rajiv Shakdher appeared for the state.
stories.background: The case arises from allegations of a cash-for-jobs racket during Balaji's tenure as Tamil Nadu's transport minister. The proceedings involve multiple chargesheets, their clubbing and the conduct of pending trials. Deccan Herald reported that the Supreme Court was hearing applications seeking completion of trials in four cases before the sessions court dealing with cases involving members of Parliament.
stories.whyItMatters: The order stops the trial court from framing charges against Balaji until the Supreme Court hears the matter, while the bench's remarks address how prosecutions are handled when governments change.

stories.headline: US Army detonates 5 tonnes of lead azide in Iowa; EPA reports no airborne lead
stories.dek: Federal officials called the controlled blast a success, but soil and surface results are not yet public and the EPA chief declined to declare the area safe.
stories.summary: The US Army destroyed about 9,700 pounds of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday, and the EPA said its air monitors detected no airborne lead. Officials have not yet reported soil or surface results.
body: The US Army detonated about 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday, and the Environmental Protection Agency said its air monitors detected no airborne lead.

The charges went off at about 9 am local time, destroying 68 barrels of the compound. Smoke rose several hundred feet and drifted south before dissipating, The Verge reported. The Army said all barrels were destroyed, with no secondary explosions or damage to infrastructure.

The EPA said in a statement that "real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region" an hour after the blast. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle wrote on social media that the detonation "exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success".
Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley told a press conference the Army had reduced the risk to residents "as close to zero as it's absolutely humanly possible", according to the Associated Press.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, speaking to CNN, called the early readings "an extraordinarily good sign" but did not declare the area safe. He said he would not do so before he could receive data and release it publicly, and he cited the EPA's assurances after the September 11 attacks that proved premature. At a later briefing, federal officials did not say whether lead had been found on surfaces or in soil, the New York Post reported.

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds called the outcome a "best-case scenario". Governor-elect Rob Sand, who takes office as her successor, said more testing was needed and called for "immediate transparency" on why the run-up was "so chaotic and unclear". He said anyone affected "must be taken care of fully, right away".
Federal Emergency Management Agency administrator Cameron Hamilton said additional resources and testing would follow in the coming days and weeks.

Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson, who watched from a workplace eight miles away, said he felt "relieved" and "vindicated". Resident Sandy Mabeus, also eight miles away, said she neither felt nor heard the blast. Farmer David Vandenberg, about 20 miles away, said he heard a rumble around nine o'clock and expected the effects to be minimal.

The Army had put in place precautions to limit lead dust, including four walls of 16,000-gallon water tanks to catch particulate. It covered the earth-covered magazines with tarps and containment screens and flooded them with foam.

Before the blast, the Army released models showing airborne lead travelling about 100 miles southwest of the site, with dust deposition across roughly 200 square miles in that direction. The EPA had about 300 staff and contractors on the ground and took roughly 1,200 samples of air, land, dust and water as baselines.
Displaced residents are being lodged until Friday, November 27, and can return once the all-clear is given.
keyFacts: The Army detonated 68 barrels holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am.
The EPA reported zero detection of airborne lead an hour after the blast.
Evacuation was voluntary within about five miles; farther residents were told to shelter in place.
Displaced residents are lodged until Friday, November 27, pending an all-clear.
EPA took roughly 1,200 baseline samples of air, land, dust and water before the blast.
stories.background:
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century and began moving away from it about 15 years ago because it is hard to transport and store. Over time the stored material crystallised and became unstable. An inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives found significant crystallisation on the barrels' exterior last March.

The detonation was first set for November 20 and was delayed three times after public opposition and a lawsuit by the Sierra Club and Iowa Environmental Council. A federal appeals court reinstated the EPA emergency permit on Monday, saying the concerns were valid but the risk of an unplanned explosion was greater.
stories.whyItMatters: Lead has no safe exposure level and is especially harmful to young children and pregnant people, so soil and surface results will determine whether residents near Middletown face any lasting risk.

stories.headline: Colombian forces storm Cartagena supermarket, free all hostages after 17 hours
stories.dek: One man police called a hostage-taker was killed and four were arrested; local media identified the dead man as a 51-year-old whose wife had been searching for him.
stories.summary: Colombian police and special forces stormed an Éxito supermarket in Cartagena early on Wednesday, freeing all remaining hostages after a siege of about 17 hours. One man was killed and four were arrested, and the circumstances of the death are disputed in local reports.
body: Colombian police and special forces stormed an Éxito supermarket in Cartagena at about 1.30am on Wednesday, freeing all remaining hostages and ending a siege of about 17 hours, police and the government said.

Armed, masked men entered the store in the La Castellana neighbourhood at about 8am on Tuesday. President Abelardo de la Espriella first put the number of hostages at 30. Police later put it at about 70, according to The Guardian; the BBC reported 76. Ten people, including elderly women, were released during the day.

Special forces broke through blocked entrances and used stun grenades, The Guardian reported. Four of the captors were arrested and one man was killed. De la Espriella said the group had been offered a chance to surrender and refused. "This operation was absolutely flawless," he said in a video, according to Reuters.

Local media identified the dead man as Haider Muñetón Zapata, 51, according to The Guardian. His wife told Blu Radio on Tuesday that he had gone to the store to buy buñuelos and stopped answering messages at 8.12am. He reportedly had no criminal record.

Cartagena Mayor Dumek Turbay told local media that Zapata allegedly resisted and attacked an officer, and police shot him. Turbay said some captors had tried to blend in with the hostages by removing hoods and changing clothes, so police screened the hostages to identify the four who were arrested. The BBC reported that the identities of those arrested had not been released.

De la Espriella said the group had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle, was spotted by private security and took refuge in the store. He said they were common criminals, not a terrorist group. Local media reported the gunmen demanded safe passage, nearly $2m and armoured vehicles, according to the BBC.

Employees described the ordeal to local media. Johan Correa said he and others were held face down with their hands tied in a cold-storage room for more than four hours. Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo said the gunmen claimed to have rigged the exits with explosives. The mayor said freed hostages were checked by medical teams before being reunited with families.

The siege fell on the 10th anniversary of the 2016 peace accord with the Farc. On Monday night a car bomb outside the Meta departmental government headquarters in Villavicencio injured more than 20 people. De la Espriella blamed a Farc dissident faction. Reuters reported no immediate claim of responsibility.
Rafael Núñez airport in Cartagena briefly suspended landings for about 45 minutes while the armed forces used a runway, Reuters reported.
keyFacts: Hostages were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday after roughly 17 hours in captivity.

stories.background: De la Espriella, in office for just over three months, is a critic of the 2016 peace accord with the Farc and has returned to a confrontational approach to armed groups, breaking with the "total peace" plan of his predecessor, Gustavo Petro. Recent days brought a car bombing in Villavicencio and an ELN drone attack in Cúcuta.
stories.whyItMatters: The identity of the man killed is unresolved in local reports, with police saying he resisted and his family saying he had gone to the store as a customer.
