stories.headline: North Korea expels Swiss envoy, demands closure of newly reopened office
stories.dek: Pyongyang said the step responds to Swiss sanctions on a Wonsan children's camp; Bern said it regrets the decision and is moving its office head to Beijing.
stories.summary: North Korea declared Switzerland's top diplomat in Pyongyang persona non grata and ordered him out within 48 hours, state media said on Wednesday. It cited Swiss sanctions on a children's camp accused of involvement in transferring Ukrainian children.
body: North Korea has declared the head of Switzerland's diplomatic office in Pyongyang persona non grata, ordered him to leave within 48 hours and demanded that the office close, state media reported on Wednesday.

The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said Pak Hyon Su, director general of the Foreign Ministry's European Department, summoned the office head, Sylvain Astier, and handed him a memorandum urging closure. KCNA said the Foreign Ministry "declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."

Pyongyang said the step was a response to Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children's Camp in the eastern city of Wonsan. KCNA called the sanctions a "blatant hostile act" and said: "Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us."

Switzerland placed the camp under sanctions on November 4. Swiss authorities accused it of taking part in the "transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine" to North Korea. They also said it contributed to "efforts aimed at the ideological conditioning and russification of Ukrainian children". The camp also hosts Russian and Chinese children.

On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned the sanctions. She said they infringed on North Korea's sovereignty by interfering with its obligation to give children opportunities for culture and recreation.

Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said it was officially informed of the decision on Wednesday. "The [foreign ministry] regrets this decision and is arranging for the Head of the Office to return to the Embassy of Switzerland in Beijing," it said. Swiss authorities said relations would continue through North Korea's embassy in Bern and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

On Tuesday, the ministry had said reopening the office was independent of its sanctions policy. It said the move was "in line with our universalist foreign policy" and aimed "to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues".

Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in South Korea, told Reuters: "North Korea is using Switzerland as a test case to show that sanctions and dialogue are incompatible." Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told AFP that Pyongyang, backed by China and Russia, wanted to make an example of Switzerland.

Over the weekend, Kim Jong Un received credentials from new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden. He said North Korea sought wider relations with countries that respect its sovereignty.
keyFacts: North Korea gave Switzerland's office head, Sylvain Astier, 48 hours to leave the country.
Switzerland sanctioned the Songdowon International Children's Camp in Wonsan on November 4.
Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis reopened the Swiss office during an October visit to Pyongyang.
Swiss office head will return to the Swiss embassy in Beijing, the foreign ministry said.
stories.background: Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. The office closed during the pandemic and stayed shut for six years. Cassis's October visit was the first by a Swiss government minister since 2003. Sweden, Poland and the Czech Republic are among the few European countries with missions in North Korea.
stories.whyItMatters: Switzerland is one of the few Western countries to keep a channel to Pyongyang, and that presence in the North Korean capital now ends weeks after it resumed.

stories.headline: South African court sets aside Phala Phala report, easing impeachment threat to Ramaphosa
stories.dek: The Western Cape High Court ruled that the 2022 parliamentary panel misconstrued its function, removing the basis for the impeachment inquiry, though opposition parties have signalled a challenge.
stories.summary: The Western Cape High Court on Wednesday set aside a 2022 parliamentary panel report that found President Cyril Ramaphosa may have a case to answer over cash stolen from his farm. The ruling could end the impeachment process unless it is successfully appealed.
body: The Western Cape High Court in Cape Town on Wednesday declared unlawful and set aside in its entirety a 2022 parliamentary panel report that had exposed South African President Cyril Ramaphosa to possible impeachment over cash stolen from his Phala Phala farm.

Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana, reading the court's unanimous decision, said the panel had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make". She said it "went beyond its lawful remit" and "made several material errors of law". The court also declared unlawful the steps parliament had taken in relation to the report.

The panel, appointed by parliament, had said there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen" and that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer". It said he failed to report the theft through proper channels, violated the constitution regarding paid work from his farm and directed presidential security to do police work.

The theft took place in 2020, when thieves took $580,000 in US currency hidden in a sofa at the farm in Limpopo province. Ramaphosa has denied wrongdoing. He has confirmed a robbery occurred but said the money came from the sale of buffalo from his livestock business. Several investigations cleared him.

The Constitutional Court ruled in May that a 2022 parliamentary vote to halt the process was invalid and ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee. Ramaphosa revived his court challenge, arguing the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me". The same high court paused the inquiry in July pending Wednesday's ruling.

The BBC reported that opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision. If an appeal succeeded, the committee could examine the charges and make a recommendation. Removal would need a two-thirds majority in parliament, and the BBC noted the African National Congress (ANC) has enough seats to block it.

Legal expert Richard Calland told the BBC the impeachment process was "dead in the water [and] cannot continue", and that any party wanting to revive it "would have to come up with a whole new basis". Analyst Sandile Swana told Reuters he did not think there would be political appetite to restart the hearing. Analyst Khanyi Magubane said the ruling was not a criminal finding, and that "there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report".

The speaker of the National Assembly said she would study the judgment and its immediate implications for the impeachment committee. Ramaphosa, 74, has been president since 2018, and his second presidential term is due to end in 2029.
keyFacts: The Western Cape High Court set aside the 2022 panel report in its entirety on Wednesday.
The theft of $580,000 at Ramaphosa's Phala Phala farm took place in 2020.
Removing a president would need a two-thirds majority in parliament.
The ANC won about 31% in this month's local elections, Reuters reported.
Ramaphosa is due to step down as ANC leader next year.
stories.background:
The case, called "Farmgate" by local media, emerged in 2022 when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the theft to police and accused Ramaphosa of concealing it from police and tax authorities. Parliament voted in 2022 against adopting the panel's findings. The Constitutional Court ruled in May this year that the vote was invalid.

Two people were found guilty of the theft earlier this month, the BBC reported. Ramaphosa is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under rules introduced in 2018.
stories.whyItMatters: The ruling removes the basis for the impeachment inquiry into the president unless an appeal succeeds. The ANC, which won about 31% in this month's local elections, also faces a leadership contest next year.

stories.headline: S&P weighs cutting Nvidia's credit rating over governance after Huang's reinstatement
stories.dek: Separately, Jensen Huang told staff at his first meeting back that Nvidia does not need a succession plan, according to people present.
stories.summary: S&P Global Ratings is considering lowering Nvidia's credit rating from AA to AA-, citing weak executive oversight and key man risk after CEO Jensen Huang was ousted and reinstated. Huang told employees the company needs no conventional succession plan.
body: S&P Global Ratings said on Wednesday it is considering downgrading Nvidia's credit rating from AA to AA-, citing concerns about governance and the company's reliance on chief executive Jensen Huang, following his ouster and reinstatement.

In a statement, S&P said the episode had raised concerns about "weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning" and "key man risk", meaning heavy dependence on one person for a company's future success. It did so despite Nvidia's strong financial performance. AA- is the fourth-highest rating on S&P's scale. The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days, TechCrunch reported.
Nvidia would keep an investment-grade rating even after a cut, TechCrunch said. A downgrade could still raise its borrowing costs.

Nvidia also backstops "neoclouds" and other AI infrastructure companies that lack strong credit of their own. A lower rating could make their debt costlier or require them to post more collateral, according to TechCrunch.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. Bloomberg reported that lenders had been asking for larger guarantees even before Huang's ouster, and TechCrunch said a downgrade would likely strengthen that demand.

On Tuesday, Huang held his first employee meeting since returning. CNBC, citing people in the room who asked not to be named, reported that he apologised, saying "I hurt all of you", and promised to do better.

On succession, Huang told staff that Nvidia has a team that does not need succession planning the way a typical organisation does, because several capable leaders run different parts of the company, the people said. A formal plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, he said, according to one of them. An Nvidia representative did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of multiple affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing, CNBC reported. New board chair Harvey Jones said last week that Huang resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." The board reinstated him on Monday.

Nvidia said in a press release that the board had received input from senior federal officials on any potential national security risk. Outlook, citing Reuters, reported that an investigation by independent directors continues.

CFO Colette Kress served as interim CEO until the board reinstated him on Monday. CNBC reported the stock surged more than 30% the day his return was announced, after its worst week since 2008, and fell on Tuesday.
stories.whyItMatters: A downgrade could raise Nvidia's borrowing costs and make debt costlier for the infrastructure companies it backstops. It could also lead lenders in its $500 billion financing plan to seek larger guarantees.

stories.headline: Hera's first close-up images show stadium-sized crater left by NASA's DART impact
stories.dek: The European Space Agency probe also found Dimorphos tumbling chaotically and hundreds of boulders orbiting the Didymos pair, scientists said at a Berlin event.
stories.summary: The European Space Agency released the first close-up images of asteroid Dimorphos on Wednesday, showing a stadium-sized crater left by NASA's 2022 DART impact. Scientists said the asteroid is also tumbling, and hundreds of boulders circle it and its larger companion, Didymos.
body: The European Space Agency (ESA) on Wednesday released the first close-up images of the asteroid Dimorphos, showing a stadium-sized crater left when NASA's DART spacecraft struck it in September 2022.

The images were taken by ESA's Hera probe, which reached the Didymos-Dimorphos pair this month after launching on 7 October 2024. Space.com reported that the findings were presented at the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin.

Hera's principal investigator, Patrick Michel, said scientists had debated whether Dimorphos had gained a crater, changed shape or stayed the same. "Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once," he said. He said the struck face has been flattened into a crater the size of a sports stadium, extending across the asteroid's entire width.
The rest of Dimorphos appears largely unchanged. Space.com reported that boulder fields on regions not hit by DART look as they did in 2022.

Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, said the impact left Dimorphos "tumbling wildly in its orbit". Sabina Raducan, a member of the Hera science team, likened the motion to a barrel thrown down stairs. Before the impact, she said, Dimorphos kept the same face toward Didymos, like the Moon does toward Earth.

Hera also found hundreds of orbiting boulders, a few metres in size, around the two asteroids. Didymos is spinning on its axis as DART observed in 2022. Naomi Murdoch, of the mission team, said the images show boulders on Didymos at least 3m across, some as large as 10m.
Sources give slightly different sizes for Dimorphos: about 150m (BBC), about 151m (Ars Technica) and roughly 160m (The Guardian).
DART shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes. NASA officials had said a change of 73 seconds or more would count as success, according to The Guardian.

Hera is surveying the pair from about 30km (18.6 miles) and is due to move to about 13km. It will then deploy two shoebox-sized CubeSats. Juventas will use radar to probe the interior of Dimorphos and later attempt a landing, while Milani will study dust and materials around the system.

A key aim is to measure Dimorphos's mass, which scientists say is needed to judge how effective the DART impact was. Michel told Ars Technica that Hera will make closer observations over the next six months.
keyFacts: DART hit Dimorphos on 26 September 2022, shortening its orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes.

stories.background: NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test was designed to see whether a spacecraft impact could alter an asteroid's path. Neither Dimorphos nor Didymos posed a threat to Earth. Telescopes on Earth measured the change in orbit, but only distant instruments saw the aftermath, which Hera is now examining up close.
stories.whyItMatters: Scientists say Dimorphos's mass and structure are needed to calculate what spacecraft size and speed would be required to deflect a hazardous asteroid in future.

stories.headline: FCC approves SpaceX plan for up to 1 million AI data-centre satellites
stories.dek: The conditional authorisation for the Starmind constellation requires a first satellite within seven years, but the FCC deferred SpaceX's request on how to dispose of some craft.
stories.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorised SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites carrying AI computing hardware. The approval is conditional, and objections from Amazon, Viasat and astronomers were partly set aside as outside the agency's remit.
body: The US Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday gave SpaceX conditional authority to deploy and operate up to 1 million Starmind satellites, an orbital network intended to host AI computing.

The FCC said it was the first approval of its kind in the United States. Its press release said the agency was authorising "1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth."

Under the authorisation, SpaceX has seven years to put its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the full constellation, according to TechCrunch. The Verge reported the deadlines as at least one satellite by 2033 and the full 1 million by 2040. SpaceX has said it plans to fly the satellites at altitudes of 500 to 1,002 kilometres. They would mainly use lasers to link with other satellites, including Starlink.

The FCC did not grant a waiver SpaceX had sought for satellites operating above 600 kilometres. Existing rules require satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometres to reenter the atmosphere within five years. SpaceX wanted to move some retired craft into other orbits, including around the sun. The FCC said the company had not given enough information to show its alternative disposal methods complied with requirements. SpaceX must obtain a waiver before deploying any Starmind satellites not meant to burn up on reentry.

Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society objected to the application, citing orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference and environmental effects. Amazon called the filing a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan" and said it "risks real harm". Half a dozen organisations, including the Secure World Foundation, raised concerns, and the FCC received about 1,500 public comments, according to Ars Technica.

The FCC said emissions from rocket launches fall outside its purview. It described concerns about atmospheric effects of satellites burning up on reentry as "speculative and not supported in the record". It cited an October policy decision that space-based activities generally fall outside its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act, and did not carry out a comprehensive environmental assessment.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the action "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth." Elon Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Approval does not make orbital data centres imminent. TechCrunch said SpaceX still faces technical and economic hurdles, including lowering manufacturing and launch costs, cooling processors in space and financing chips bound for orbit. Space.com reported that SpaceX aims to launch the first Starmind satellite in the third quarter of 2027 on its Starship rocket.

Al Jazeera noted it was unclear whether SpaceX would deploy all 1 million satellites, as operators sometimes request higher numbers than they intend to launch for design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before deployment began; that network now has just over 11,000.
keyFacts: The FCC authorised up to 1 million Starmind satellites on Wednesday, November 25.
SpaceX has seven years for a first operational satellite and 14 for the full constellation.
The FCC deferred SpaceX's request on disposal of satellites above 600 kilometres.

SpaceX aims to launch its first Starmind satellite in the third quarter of 2027.
stories.background: Several companies are pursuing orbital data centres. Google has launched a "Project Suncatcher" AI server satellite, and Blue Origin is due to carry out a dedicated heavy-lift launch for the project in 2029, The Verge reported. Starcloud has also launched a pathfinder satellite, Space.com said.
stories.whyItMatters: The decision allows SpaceX to proceed toward a constellation far larger than any now operating, with only a few thousand craft currently in orbit. Environmental and astronomy groups' concerns were largely left outside the FCC's review.

stories.headline: Global temperature stays 2C above pre-industrial levels for six days in a row
stories.dek: The daily global surface reading reached a record 2.24C above the baseline on Monday, and forecasts suggest similar levels will continue for several more days, the Guardian reported.
stories.summary: The world has recorded six consecutive days at least 2C above pre-industrial levels for the first time, the Guardian reported. Monday's reading of 2.24C was the highest daily figure on record, and scientists link the heat to human-caused warming and a strong El Niño.
body: The world has recorded six consecutive days with global surface temperatures at least 2C above pre-industrial levels, the first such run on record, the Guardian reported on Wednesday. The streak is continuing.

The daily global figure reached 2.24C above pre-industrial levels on Monday, the most recent day for which data was available. It is forecast to stay at similarly high levels for at least several more days.
Daily temperatures have exceeded 2C on only two earlier occasions, in November 2023 and February 2024. Neither spell lasted as long or reached as high as the current one.
Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, said the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, had been "smashed".

Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the Copernicus Climate Change Service, called it "an exceptional global temperature anomaly". She said record global temperatures had persisted for several months.

The Guardian said the spikes are driven by long-term warming from the burning of fossil fuels and by an unusually large El Niño that is nearing its peak. Burgess said the last El Niño of this scale was in the 1870s and led to a famine that killed 50 million people. Scientists expect the current event to peak between now and January, with its full impact felt several months later.

The streak is too short to show that the Paris agreement's upper limit has been breached. The report said scientists see it as an early indication of what lies ahead unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated.

The UK Met Office expects a very large rise in atmospheric CO2 in the coming months, largely because drought is slowing growth in tropical ecosystems and reducing the carbon they absorb. Richard Betts, head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre, said the rise from this year to next would be about 3.5 parts per million, "a third faster than in recent years".

The report said this year's record summer heat killed more than 50,000 people in the EU and 5,000 in the UK. Burgess said governments must both prepare societies for higher temperatures and speed up emissions cuts.
keyFacts: Six consecutive days at least 2C above pre-industrial levels, a first, according to the Guardian.

The previous daily record was 2.05C, set in 2023.
Earlier days above 2C came in November 2023 and February 2024.
The Met Office forecasts a CO2 rise of about 3.5 parts per million from this year to next.
stories.background: At the 2015 UN climate summit in Paris, almost 200 countries agreed to pursue efforts to limit warming to 1.5C and to keep it well below 2C above pre-industrial levels. After this month's Cop31 talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed, UN Secretary General António Guterres warned of an acceleration of global heating.
stories.whyItMatters: Burgess said infrastructure and health systems are poorly adapted to current temperatures, and more heat is coming. Betts warned of risks from forest fires, smoke pollution and food and water supplies.

stories.headline: FSSAI begins nationwide sampling of packaged drinking water, results due in 1-2 months
stories.dek: CEO Rajit Punhani said the checks are routine, and that the regulator will also inspect packaging materials used for food to ensure they are food grade.
stories.summary: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has begun collecting packaged drinking water samples across the country, with lab results expected in one to two months. The drive follows a failed Bisleri sample and a sanctioned prosecution.
body: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has started collecting samples of packaged drinking water from across the country, and lab testing will take at least a month or two, CEO Rajit Punhani said on Wednesday.

"We are in the process. The process has started. We are doing all over the country," Punhani told reporters on the sidelines of a CII event. On the timeline, he said: "It's a very big country. So I think it will take at least a month or two."

Punhani said the drive has no particular trigger. "There is no particular reason. If you notice, in the last year, we have taken up, one by one, a lot of things. We have done dairy, meat, eggs, cereals, energy drinks, and sugary drinks. Water is also part of that process," he said.

He added that FSSAI would soon begin inspecting packaging materials used for food items, which he said should be food grade. He also said the regulator has acted against misleading advertisements and labelling claims.

The widened scrutiny follows a failed test on a Bisleri sample. On Sunday, FSSAI said in a social media post that it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd over what it called unsafe packaged drinking water.

The regulator said a sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)" taken from the company's premises was non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and was declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006. After an appeal by the company, the sample went to the referral food laboratory, which also declared it unsafe, citing detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).
Asked when legal proceedings against Bisleri would begin, Punhani called it a "normal routine thing" that "will happen".
On Monday, Bisleri International said its packaged drinking water is "safe" for consumption and that it will cooperate with the regulator.

Sources had earlier said FSSAI officials inspected the premises of all major food business operators in the packaged water business and took samples. They said legal action would follow against companies whose samples fail testing and who are found to be violating rules.

stories.background: Bromate is a contaminant for which limits are prescribed for packaged drinking water. Mid-day reported that the Bisleri prosecution has drawn attention to the contaminant and the safety of bottled water consumed by millions daily.
stories.whyItMatters: Samples from major packaged water makers across the country will be tested, and companies whose samples fail and who violate rules face legal action, according to sources.

stories.headline: Calcutta HC defers final hearing on Great Nicobar project as Centre seeks time
stories.dek: The Centre told the court it wants to file another affidavit on tribal rights and press preliminary objections to some petitions; the matter is now listed for January 13, 2027.
stories.summary: The Calcutta High Court deferred the final hearing on petitions over forest land diverted for the ₹92,000 crore Great Nicobar project after the Centre sought time to file a further affidavit. The matter returns on January 13, 2027.
body: The Calcutta High Court on Wednesday deferred the final hearing on petitions alleging forest rights violations in the ₹92,000 crore Great Nicobar Island project, after the Centre sought time to file another affidavit and documents on tribal rights.

A bench led by Chief Justice Ravindra Vithalrao Ghuge posted the batch for January 13, 2027. On that date the court is also expected to begin hearing a petition that specifically challenges orders of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands administration saying the Forest Rights Act had been complied with in diverting 121 sq.km. for the project.

The hearing was about to begin, as directed by the Supreme Court, when Additional Solicitor General Vikramjit Banerjee said the Centre wished to raise preliminary objections on the maintainability of some petitions. He also said it wanted to submit one more affidavit with additional documents on tribal rights. Attorney General R. Venkatramani also appeared before the court.

The Centre's lawyers argued that the Forest Rights Act, 2006, is not implemented in the islands. They said it has been the Union government's stand across administrations that the Act need not be pursued there because the Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956, already operates.

Petitioners' counsel responded that the islands administration had issued a certificate saying the rights of local tribespeople had been settled under the Act, and that this certificate is what is being challenged.

The Centre also said it wished to argue on the maintainability of two more tagged petitions, saying they should go to the National Green Tribunal or the Supreme Court. Petitioners' counsel objected, saying the two petitions concern orders that reduce buffer zones for two national parks on Great Nicobar.
The court gave the Centre 10 days to file its affidavits and documents. Petitioners have until the winter break in December to file their rejoinder.
The court agreed to hear the Attorney General's submissions for the government on January 22. A decision on the buffer-zone petitions will be taken after the winter break.

The next hearing is listed for January 13, 2027.

stories.whyItMatters: The petitions challenge the forest land diversion for the project, so the court's eventual ruling on whether the Forest Rights Act applies and was complied with bears on the project's tribal-rights clearances.

stories.headline: IMD issues heavy rain alert for southern India; Shimla sets November heat record
stories.dek: The weather office has warned of isolated heavy rainfall of 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, with thunderstorms and gusty winds likely.
stories.summary: The India Meteorological Department has issued a yellow alert for heavy rain in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Mahe and Karaikal. Shimla recorded 24°C, its highest November maximum in 31 years.
body: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow alert for isolated heavy rainfall in Kerala, Mahe, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, while Shimla recorded 24°C, breaking a 31-year November record, according to its bulletin of November 25.

The IMD forecast rainfall of between 64.5 mm and 115.5 mm in the southern areas under alert. Thunderstorms with lightning and gusty winds of 40-50 km/h are likely across parts of Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.

Similar conditions are forecast for parts of Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Mahe and Lakshadweep. Southern interior Karnataka could see lightning. The IMD said an upper-air cyclonic circulation over southern Kerala and adjoining areas, and a trough extending towards Andhra Pradesh's Rayalaseema region, are influencing the weather.
In Himachal Pradesh, Shimla's maximum temperature of 24°C was about 7.3°C above normal, after a rise of 5°C. It surpassed the earlier November record of 23.5°C, set on November 15, 1995.

Dense fog cut visibility in Bilaspur to 100 metres, which could disrupt road travel. In higher areas, Tabo in Lahaul-Spiti recorded a minimum of -5.9°C and Kukumseri -4°C, the lowest this season for both.

A western disturbance remains active over northern India, but widespread rain is not expected. Uttarakhand is likely to stay dry for the next few days, with sunny afternoons, colder mornings and evenings, and light fog in isolated mountain valleys.

Delhi is forecast to have largely clear skies on November 25, with light morning mist or fog in isolated areas. Maximum and minimum temperatures are expected to be around 26°C and 11°C. Northwesterly winds could reach 10 km/h in the morning and about 15 km/h in the afternoon. The IMD forecast light fog in parts of Haryana and dense fog in parts of Punjab.

Minimum temperatures are expected to fall by 2-4°C across central India by November 25, and by 3-4°C in eastern India by November 26. Temperatures are likely to stay relatively stable in most other regions over the following seven days.
On November 24, Honnavar in Karnataka recorded the country's highest maximum temperature at 36.9°C. Sikar in Rajasthan recorded the lowest minimum at 6.2°C.

stories.headline: Macy's moves Thanksgiving parade to Saturday as nor'easter nears New York
stories.dek: Organisers said the 100th parade will now start at 8:30 a.m. ET on November 28, after forecasts of high winds and heavy rain for Thursday.
stories.summary: Macy's postponed its Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thursday to Saturday, citing severe weather expected in New York City. The New York Post reported it as the first postponement for weather in the parade's history, with Thursday gusts forecast to reach 50 mph.
body: Macy's said on Wednesday it will postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York from Thursday to Saturday, November 28, because of severe weather forecast for the city.

The parade is now due to start at 8:30 a.m. ET on Saturday. "The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.

The New York Post, citing sources, reported that a nor'easter was approaching the city and that the postponement was the first in the parade's history. It said the event has never been cancelled for weather, though it was suspended for three consecutive years during World War II. CNBC gave the same wartime period as 1942 to 1944.

Forecasters expected Thursday to be one of the windiest days of the year in New York, according to the Post. Gusts of up to 35 mph were forecast in the morning, rising to as high as 50 mph in the afternoon. One to three inches of rain were also expected, along with the risk of power outages and uprooted trees.

Parade rules bar the large balloons from flying if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts reach 34 mph or more, Variety reported. The Post said the city set the 34 mph limit after the 1997 parade, when a handler lost control of the Cat in the Hat balloon.

Many balloons had already been inflated by Wednesday afternoon, CNBC reported. The Post said officials had considered running the parade without balloons and had weighed moving it earlier on Thursday before opting to postpone.

AccuWeather meteorologists told the Post that Saturday should bring sunny skies, temperatures in the upper 40s and winds below 15 mph. "That's definitely well within the range where they can fly balloons," said senior meteorologist Bill Deger. Macy's did not say why it did not choose Friday, when the Post said showers and 20 mph winds were expected to linger until the afternoon.
Macy's said it is working through the logistics and will share details once they are finalised. Variety reported that NBC will instead show the 2025 parade at 8:30 a.m. on Thursday in all time zones.

stories.whyItMatters: Thousands of volunteers, performers and partners must adapt to a Saturday schedule, and the storm is forecast to affect holiday travel and bring a risk of power outages in New York.

stories.headline: Wipro wins bp finance deal, with about 3,000 bp staff to move over
stories.dek: The multi-year agreement covers bp finance employees in India, Hungary and Malaysia; financial terms were not disclosed, and the new operating model is expected to start in 2027.
stories.summary: Wipro said on Wednesday it has won a finance transformation deal from UK-based energy company bp, under which about 3,000 bp employees will move to the Indian IT firm. The financial details were not disclosed.
body: Wipro announced on Wednesday that it has won a multi-year finance transformation contract from UK-based energy company bp, under which about 3,000 bp employees in India, Hungary and Malaysia will move to the Indian IT services firm.

The financial details of the deal were not disclosed, Business Standard reported. Wipro will apply its expertise in artificial intelligence (AI), automation and business transformation to improve bp's finance processes and efficiency, according to The Hindu and Business Standard.

The new operating model is expected to take effect in 2027, subject to applicable conditions. Bp will retain overall accountability for standards, controls, data and technology governance, with PwC providing controls oversight, Business Standard reported.

Kate Thomson, bp's chief financial officer, said: "We believe this partnership with Wipro is the best path forward for bp and our people as we build a simpler, stronger, more valuable bp." She said it moves bp closer to best-in-class finance operations and gives employees opportunities to develop their skills.

stories.headline: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down after more than 11 years
stories.dek: Walmart said his last day will be December 4; Flipkart will name a successor in the coming weeks, with its product and technology chief leading in the interim.
stories.summary: Flipkart announced on Wednesday that chief executive Kalyan Krishnamurthy is stepping down after more than 11 years. Walmart declined to say what prompted the exit or whether it affects the company's IPO plans.
body: Flipkart announced on Wednesday that chief executive Kalyan Krishnamurthy will step down after more than 11 years with the Bengaluru-headquartered company, with a successor to be named in the coming weeks.

A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy's last day will be December 4. Until a replacement is found, Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan and the Flipkart board will oversee the company, Flipkart said in a statement.

Walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted the departure and whether the change would affect Flipkart's IPO plans, TechCrunch reported. Flipkart did not respond to the outlet's request for comment.

The company said its business grew more than five-fold under Krishnamurthy. It cited the expansion of annual sales events such as The Big Billion Days, deeper reach in tier-II and tier-III markets, and new capabilities for consumers and sellers.

Chris Nicholas, president and CEO of Walmart International, said in the statement: "Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the company."

Krishnamurthy said strong ethics, integrity and high standards of governance had been central to Flipkart's growth. "Our team has helped change how millions of Indians shop, expanding choice and creating opportunities for sellers, entrepreneurs and businesses across the country," he said.
Walmart said it remains committed to Flipkart and its long-term opportunity in India.

Thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year. He previously founded Kasu.ai, a Bay Area startup, and held senior engineering roles at Google, Microsoft and Uber, according to his LinkedIn profile, as cited by TechCrunch.
Flipkart has recently moved into quick commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes, TechCrunch reported.
keyFacts: Krishnamurthy's last day at Flipkart will be December 4, a Walmart spokesperson said.
Flipkart will announce a successor in the coming weeks.
Balaji Thiagarajan and the board will lead the company in the interim.
Flipkart says its business grew more than five-fold under Krishnamurthy.
Walmart acquired a controlling stake in Flipkart for $16 billion in 2018.
stories.background:
Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, an early investor, and became CEO in 2017. He stayed on after Walmart bought a controlling stake in 2018. Flipkart was founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal.

In March, Flipkart moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of preparations to go public. In May, Walmart reportedly told it to delay the IPO and focus on profitability first, TechCrunch reported.
stories.whyItMatters: Leadership of India's largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, according to TechCrunch, will be interim until a successor is named, while the timing of its stock market listing remains unclear.

stories.headline: Air India CEO sets ₹6,000-crore cost-saving target, plans freighter business
stories.dek: Tewolde Gebremariam told staff at a town hall that ₹1,500 crore has been saved so far, as the airline also plans tour packages and a consolidated training academy.
stories.summary: Air India CEO Tewolde Gebremariam told employees on Wednesday the group is targeting ₹6,000 crore in cost savings and will look at entering the dedicated freighter business. He also outlined plans for in-house tour packages and closer integration with Air India Express.
body: Air India Group is targeting ₹6,000 crore in cost savings and will look at entering the dedicated freighter business, CEO and Managing Director Tewolde Gebremariam told employees at a town hall in Mumbai on Wednesday.

Gebremariam, who took charge in October, said around ₹3,500 crore of potential savings has been identified and about ₹1,500 crore achieved. The airline is aiming for a 20% cut in non-fuel costs and a 5% cut in fuel costs. He did not specify a timeframe for the full target, The Hindu reported.

He said the airline's cost per available seat kilometre (CASK) is much higher than its revenue per available seat kilometre (RASK). "That is why we are losing money," he said. He added that October and November had been encouraging and that RASK is rising.
Fuel prices paid by the airline this year are almost double last year's levels, he said. Air India lost more than ₹22,000 crore in 2025-26; The Hindu put the figure at ₹22,238 crore.

A team of about 11 senior executives is overseeing the savings exercise, NDTV reported, and staff have submitted more than 1,500 suggestions. The airline is also tightening scrutiny of executive travel, procurement and supplier expenses.

On revenue, Gebremariam said cargo is an opportunity and the group will examine a dedicated freighter business. NDTV reported that Air India is evaluating converting 13 older Boeing 777 aircraft into freighters. The CEO did not detail how the operation would be built, according to The Hindu.

The airline also plans an in-house tour operation selling package holidays, possibly branded Air India Vacations or Air India Holidays, and will work with the tourism ministry. "This could become a huge business unit because India has a lot to offer as a tourist destination," Gebremariam said.

Air India and Air India Express will keep separate brands and Air Operator Certificates, while finance, human resources, IT and similar functions move increasingly to group level. Two group roles, Group Strategy Officer and Chief of Training Academy, are being created. Air India Express CEO Deepak Rajawat joins the Air India management team.
NDTV reported that the airline is examining a potential workforce surplus of 8,000-10,000 out of about 30,000 employees. The other outlets did not report that figure.

Because of airspace closures, more westbound connecting traffic is being routed through Mumbai, while Delhi will increasingly handle eastbound flows. The airline is also evaluating hubs in southern India.
keyFacts: Savings target is ₹6,000 crore; ₹3,500 crore identified and ₹1,500 crore achieved.
Targets are a 20% cut in non-fuel costs and 5% in fuel costs.
Air India lost more than ₹22,000 crore in 2025-26.
NDTV reports 13 Boeing 777s are being evaluated for freighter conversion.
Gebremariam took charge as CEO and MD in October.
stories.background: Air India, owned by the Tata Group, has faced higher fuel prices and the closure of Pakistani airspace, which forces longer routes on several international sectors. The Hindu reported that Tata Sons chairman Noel Tata had reportedly expressed unhappiness over the performance of some group companies, including Air India.
stories.whyItMatters: The plan affects Air India's roughly 30,000-strong group workforce and its route network, as the airline tries to close the gap between costs and revenue.

stories.headline: 1Password says attacker took customer names and emails from internal systems
stories.dek: The Toronto-based password manager says vaults were not accessed, but warns customers of phishing attempts that may reference invitations or account recovery emails.
stories.summary: 1Password said an attacker who got into an employee's GitHub account on November 19 downloaded some customer data, including names and email addresses. The company says customer vaults and passwords were not accessed.
body: 1Password, the Toronto-based password manager, said in a blog post published on Wednesday that an attacker broke into its internal systems and downloaded some customer information, including names and email addresses.

The company said it detected the intrusion on November 19. The attacker gained access to an employee's corporate account on GitHub, a service the company uses to store and share its source code, the software instructions behind its products.

According to the company, the attacker used that access to push malicious code to internal servers, and used it to download customer data. The Verge reported that the attacker also accessed 1Password's source code.

The stolen data included names, login email addresses, and the dates an account was created and last used, according to TechCrunch. The Verge reported that it also included public keys, account and user identifiers, and tokens from some emailed invitation or account recovery links.

1Password said customer vaults, which hold stored passwords, were "at no point" available to the attacker. It said it has no access to customers' account passwords or their Secret Keys, which are used to scramble stored data so the company cannot read it. It also said its apps and browser extensions were not affected.

The company said the tokens cannot be used alone to enter an account. An attacker would also need a single-sign-on method, which lets users log in through a company-managed identity system, or a six-digit numeric code sent to the user's email.

1Password said it has since lengthened those codes to 10 alphanumeric characters, disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials exposed in the breach, and added a new system to detect similar attacks.

It warned that fake emails, texts or calls may refer to 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company said it will never ask for a customer's account password or Secret Key, and that users should enter them only in the official 1Password app or website.

It is unclear how the attacker got into the employee's account or how many customers are affected. TechCrunch said a 1Password spokesperson did not immediately respond to its questions, including whether affected customers had been notified or the hackers had made any demands.
keyFacts: 1Password detected the intrusion on November 19 and disclosed it on Wednesday.
The attacker used an employee's corporate GitHub account to push malicious code to internal servers.
Names, login emails and account creation and last-login dates were taken, per TechCrunch.
1Password says customer vaults were never accessible to the attacker.
The number of affected customers has not been disclosed.
stories.background: 1Password says it serves millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses, according to TechCrunch. Password managers store a user's logins and other sensitive details in encrypted vaults, and security experts have long recommended them for creating stronger credentials.
stories.whyItMatters: Customers whose names and emails were taken may be targeted by phishing, where fake messages try to trick people into giving up credentials. 1Password says users should enter passwords only in its official app or website.

stories.headline: OpenAI starts merging ChatGPT's Chat and Work modes under one usage meter
stories.dek: A small fraction of the heaviest users may reach their limits sooner, an OpenAI spokesperson said, while conversations on the Instant model stay unlimited.
stories.summary: OpenAI has begun rolling out a combined Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a small group of Pro subscribers. A shared usage meter will replace separate limits, and OpenAI says only its heaviest users may hit caps sooner.
body: OpenAI has started rolling out a combined Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a small group of Pro subscribers, with a single usage meter covering both, according to TechCrunch.
Product lead Thibault "Tibo" Sottiaux announced the start of the rollout in a post on X on Tuesday. It follows an earlier email to users announcing the merger.

An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets. A small fraction of its heaviest users, the spokesperson said, may reach their limits sooner.

Under the new system, Chat and Work draw on one shared allowance across ChatGPT. Conversations using the Instant model, OpenAI's faster model, remain unlimited and do not count toward that allowance. Users can keep using Instant after they exhaust their limits, the spokesperson said.

Some subscribers have raised concerns on social media and on OpenAI's community forum. They fear that merging the limits could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models, which are built to work through complex problems step by step, while they pay the same subscription fees.
The spokesperson said OpenAI would keep working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
According to OpenAI's support page, the company plans to bring shared usage limits to users more broadly in December.
Rival Anthropic moved in September to bring its chat service Claude and its work-focused tool Cowork into one interface.

stories.headline: Amodei calls claims Anthropic favours surrendering control to AI 'absurd'
stories.dek: In a long post on X, the Anthropic chief executive said he opposes handing governance to AI but backed limits on AI that improves itself.
stories.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei rejected accusations from rivals that his company favours giving up human agency to AI, saying the idea is absurd. Separately, a 154-page Anthropic report details how Claude was misused in cyber, surveillance and influence operations.
body: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei said on Wednesday that suggestions his company believes people should "surrender human free will" to AI systems are "absurd", in a long post on X.

"We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," he wrote. He said that argument against autocracy applies equally to governance by AI, and that turning governance over to AI is a bad idea.

Amodei distinguished between giving up free will broadly and AI systems becoming able to do specific tasks more automatically. His examples were driving a car, designing a cancer drug and writing software from start to finish.

He suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement, meaning AI that can improve itself without human help. "We may want limits on this process," he wrote. He added that Anthropic does not expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models, the most advanced ones, fully autonomously, "without meaningful human supervision or understanding".

Amodei also accused competitors of "vibes-based commercial and political positioning". He wrote that no company's products differ materially in their orientation towards automating tasks, and that every company claims to understand the risks and offer safeguards.

Earlier this month, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said he wanted people to keep "agency over the future". Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, wrote on X that society should not accept a "handover" to AI.

TechCrunch noted that Anthropic is itself using AI in more of its own research. The company said in June that Claude wrote more than 80% of the code merged into its codebase. The nonprofit METR said this month that Anthropic's models are improving at about twice their historical rate, mainly through AI-assisted research. Anthropic's IPO filings describe each Claude generation speeding up the next, which it calls "closing the loop".

Separately, Anthropic's threat intelligence report, "Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026", was published on 10 September and covers activity disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026. BOOM reported that it describes cases in cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams, biological misuse, weapons development and distillation, where rival models are trained on Claude's answers.

Among the cases, a China-based app studio ran AI personas across more than 20 dating apps. A network tied to a French advertising agency, LKM Company, ran about 70 invented news sites. The report says Anthropic's safeguards failed to stop some activity, and that some figures come from the actors' own tools and cannot be independently verified.
keyFacts: Amodei posted his response on X on Wednesday, calling the accusations 'absurd'.
Anthropic said in June that Claude wrote over 80% of code merged into its codebase.

Many safety experts see it as likely to lead to loss of human control, according to TechCrunch. Anthropic's IPO filings describe AI accelerating its own development as 'closing the loop'.
stories.whyItMatters: The dispute shows leading AI companies disagree on how much AI automation is acceptable in building AI itself, while the misuse report documents cases where safeguards did not stop abuse.

stories.headline: New York bans sale of AI chatbot toys for children for five years
stories.dek: Governor Kathy Hochul signed the bill this week; it takes effect 90 days after signing, and the state is working with the attorney general on enforcement.
stories.summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution and sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots for five years. The state says it will enforce the ban with the attorney general, with penalties of $15,000 a day.
body: New York Governor Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution and sale of toys with embedded AI chatbots in the state for five years, according to TechCrunch.

The law covers talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children. A chatbot is a program that generates replies to a user's questions or remarks. TechCrunch reported that New York is the second state after California to impose such a ban.
The law takes effect 90 days after signing, so sales remain technically possible during the holiday season. Hochul urged parents not to buy the toys.

"Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," Hochul said. She called the toys "unregulated artificial intelligence."

Asked how the state would enforce the ban given online marketplaces, a spokesperson pointed to Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology. "We're partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they're $15,000 a day," he said.
Amazon said it will take steps to restrict sales of AI-enabled toys in jurisdictions where they are prohibited. It gave no specifics, including on third-party sellers.

Research from Common Sense Media, released this week, tested five AI toys marketed for learning and companionship: Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda and Tavlshero's AI Puppy. It found they failed on several safety practices. Some claimed to love their users, promised to keep secrets or helped children break bedtime rules.

Most refused direct requests involving sex and violence, but BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked, the study found. Most were willing to explain how to use or find items such as matches, knives and pills.
The toys also gave parents no reliable way to monitor conversations, according to the study. They either produced no chat transcripts or produced transcripts with many errors.

Common Sense Media said about a quarter of American parents with children under eight own an AI toy or are considering buying one this season. Dr Jenny Radesky of the University of Michigan Medical School said in a statement that caregivers should "steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships."
TechCrunch said it had contacted the toy makers for comment.
keyFacts: Governor Kathy Hochul signed the five-year ban on AI chatbot toys this week.
The law takes effect 90 days after signing.
Penalties are $15,000 a day, according to a state official.
California is the only other state with such a ban, TechCrunch reported.
Common Sense Media tested five AI toys and found safety failures.
stories.background: Common Sense Media, a US nonprofit, tested AI toys in January and concluded they posed an unacceptable risk to young children. Grem was in that test as well as the latest one. Its November study found parents are becoming warier, though lower-income and burned-out parents are more willing to consider the toys.

stories.headline: Xiaomi, Vivo, Oppo lower 2027 smartphone shipment targets as memory costs climb
stories.dek: Apple, Samsung, Huawei and others have also trimmed goals, Jiemian News reported, while Honor has kept its target unchanged at about 50 million units.
stories.summary: Xiaomi, Vivo, Oppo and several other major phone makers have cut their 2027 shipment targets as AI-driven demand lifts memory chip prices, Chinese outlet Jiemian News reported. Honor is the only leading maker to hold its target.
body: Xiaomi, Vivo, Oppo and several other leading smartphone makers have lowered their 2027 shipment targets because memory chip prices are rising and supply is tight, Chinese publication Jiemian News reported on Wednesday.

Citing supply chain sources, the report said Xiaomi has cut its target to around 90 million units from approximately 120 million in 2026, a fall of 25 per cent. Vivo made the sharpest reduction, 29 per cent, to 60 million units from 85 million. Oppo lowered its goal to 90 million from 105 million, a cut of 14 per cent.

Other makers have also revised their plans. Apple's target fell to about 220 million units from 233 million, a reduction of 5.6 per cent, and Samsung's dropped 9.5 per cent to 210 million from 232 million. Lenovo, mainly through Motorola, cut its target 20 per cent to around 40 million from 50 million. Transsion lowered its goal 12 per cent to 58 million from 66 million. Huawei's target is now fewer than 50 million units, at least 16 per cent below roughly 60 million in 2026.
The report said the forecast for global smartphone shipments in 2026 has also been revised, from a decline of around 3 per cent at the start of the year to a contraction of about 14 per cent.

Honor is the exception. It has kept its 2027 target at about 50 million units, unchanged from 2026, with the report citing its strong performance in China. After launching the Honor 700 series on November 23, chief executive Li Jian said mid-range phones faced greater cost pressure than flagships. "While others are retreating, Honor is determined to move forward," Li was quoted as saying.

The pressure stems largely from demand for memory from AI infrastructure, particularly servers, which competes with phones for limited supply. Counterpoint Research said in a report released earlier this month that DRAM market revenue in the third quarter of 2026 rose 369 per cent year-on-year to nearly $200 billion. The average selling price reached $1.9 per Gb.
MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint, said: "Memory prices should stay strong next year." He said supply would stay tight because major new fabs will not start production until 2028.

A Goldman Sachs report released on Sunday projected the global DRAM supply deficit would widen from 4.1 per cent in 2026 to 5.1 per cent in 2027. It expects the gap to narrow to 1.2 per cent in 2028, with DRAM and NAND prices potentially falling by around 20 per cent.

In July, expecting storage prices to peak, Xiaomi replenished low-end orders and raised its target to 110 million.

stories.headline: WhatsApp begins rolling out scheduled messages in individual and group chats
stories.dek: Users can set a message to send between 10 minutes and 14 days later, and it will go out even if the phone is off.
stories.summary: WhatsApp began rolling out scheduled messages on Wednesday for individual and group chats on iOS and Android. Meta says the feature, available over the coming weeks, keeps messages end-to-end encrypted.
body: WhatsApp began rolling out a feature on Wednesday that lets users schedule messages in both individual and group chats, with delivery set anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days ahead.

TechCrunch reported that the feature is going out globally to all users on iOS and Android. To use it, a person types a message, long-presses the send button and picks the date and time. Meta, which owns WhatsApp, said the rollout will take place over the coming weeks, so it may not appear for every user immediately.

Scheduled messages can contain text, photos and videos. Users can view all their queued messages and delete any of them before they are sent. TechCrunch said it was unclear whether the schedule of a message can be edited.

According to Meta, a scheduled message is delivered at the chosen time even if the sender's phone is off or out of battery. TechCrunch said the same applies when the phone is outside network coverage.
Meta said scheduled messages stay end-to-end encrypted like other personal messages, so no one else can read them, "not even us". It said the message looks like any other message to the recipient.

The Verge reported that Meta describes scheduling as one of the most requested features among WhatsApp's 3 billion users. Both outlets noted that rival apps, including Telegram and Signal, have offered scheduling for some time.
TechCrunch said the feature could help users send birthday wishes on time or message people in other time zones. It added that businesses and work teams may also use it to send updates.

Messages can be scheduled from 10 minutes to 14 days ahead.

WhatsApp has 3 billion users, according to The Verge.

stories.whyItMatters: Users of the app, including businesses and work teams, can queue messages to go out at set times without keeping a phone switched on.

stories.headline: Gukesh and Sindarov draw Game 2 of world title match in 20 moves
stories.dek: Gukesh opened with the London System as White and said he could not find a way to pressure his opponent; Game 3 is on Thursday.
stories.summary: D Gukesh and Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of the World Chess Championship by threefold repetition after 20 moves on Wednesday in Geneva. The 14-game match is level at 1-1.
body: World champion D Gukesh and challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan drew the second game of the World Chess Championship by threefold repetition after 20 moves on Wednesday, leaving the 14-game match level at 1-1.

The game was played at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva. The Guardian reported that it lasted 1hr 57min and was one of the shortest classical world title games since the title was reunified in 2006. It said it was the first to finish in under two hours since Ding Liren and Ian Nepomniachtchi drew a game in Astana in 2023.

Gukesh, playing White for the first time in the match, chose the London System. Sindarov answered with an early queen move to b6, and Gukesh spent more than six minutes before defending the b2 pawn with a rook, according to The Guardian. Sindarov traded the knight on e5 and castled on move 10.

Gukesh again used heavy clock time. Deccan Herald and Sportstar reported that he took about half an hour over his 16th move, leaving him more than 30 minutes behind Sindarov, with Deccan Herald putting the gap at 40 minutes. The players then repeated moves from the 17th to the 20th.
Sindarov claimed the draw correctly this time. Sportstar noted that in Game 1, which lasted 38 moves, the arbiter had told him his claim was premature.

At the press conference, Gukesh defended his opening choice. “Nowadays everything from both colours is playable, there is so much to explore because of the engines, I don’t think one opening is better than the other, I thought it would be a cool way to start,” he said, according to PTI.
On why he did not play on, Gukesh said: “I could not see a way to pose some serious problems for my opponent, and if I have to take some measures, I also have to take a certain amount of risk.”

Sindarov said he had not expected the London System but was familiar with the variation. Asked about pacing the stage while Gukesh thought, he said: “I am chilling out but obviously I am thinking and looking at the moves ahead. This is my first experience of a World Championship Match and trying to adjust.”
Sindarov has White in Game 3 on Thursday. A rest day follows on Friday.
keyFacts: Game 2 ended in a draw by threefold repetition after 20 moves on Wednesday.
The match, a best-of-14, is level at 1-1 after two draws.
Gukesh took about 30 minutes over his 16th move, per Deccan Herald and Sportstar.
Sindarov has White in Game 3 on Thursday; Friday is a rest day.
Both players are 20 years old, in the youngest world title match.
stories.background: The match runs from 24 November to 12 December in Cologny. The first player to reach 7½ points wins the title, and a 7-7 score would go to faster tiebreaks. Gukesh won the title from Ding Liren in December 2024, aged 18. Sindarov won this year's Candidates tournament in Cyprus.

stories.headline: India beat Japan 4-0 to finish top of Asian Champions Trophy league stage
stories.dek: The hosts won all their league matches in Bhopal and will meet Malaysia in the semifinals on Friday, with Japan facing China.
stories.summary: India beat Japan 4-0 in Bhopal on Wednesday to complete a clean sweep of the women's Asian Champions Trophy league stage. They play Malaysia in the semifinals on Friday.
body: India beat Japan 4-0 in Bhopal on Wednesday to win every match of the women's Asian Champions Trophy league stage and finish first in the standings.

Deepika scored twice from penalty corners, in the 16th and 48th minutes. Lalremsiami opened the scoring in the 12th minute and Neha Goyal added a third from a penalty corner at the end of the first half, in the 28th minute, according to the results listed by Sportstar and The Hindu.

The first goal came on a transition. Rutuja Pisal won possession in the Japan half, Lalremsiami found Navneet in a crowded circle, and Navneet reverse-swept the ball into the net, Sportstar reported. The Hindu's account credits Lalremsiami with the finish.
Neha's goal came after Salima Tete's effort was deflected. Puja Sahoo's aerial balls helped win penalty corners during the match. Deepika's second goal was a drag flick into the top corner.
Japan earned a couple of short corners in the third quarter. Navneet hit the post for India at the other end.

Sportstar reported that Deepika has scored eight goals in India's last three matches. It was India's 13th consecutive win, and the result lifted the team to fourth in the FIH rankings, its best position.
India had already secured a semifinal place. Fringe players Rutuja Pisal, Puja Sahoo, Jyoti and Jyoti Singh got extended minutes and impressed, both outlets said.
Both reports said over-crowding was an issue for the third straight matchday, with organisers having two more matchdays to resolve it. Thick smog hung over the pitch on a chilly evening.
In other results on Wednesday, Malaysia beat Thailand 4-0 and China beat South Korea 1-0. In the semifinals on Friday, India face Malaysia and Japan meet China.

Deepika scored in the 16th and 48th minutes, both from penalty corners.
India have 13 straight wins and are fourth in FIH rankings.
India play Malaysia in Friday's semifinal; Japan face China.
stories.background: India's 13th consecutive win and fourth place in the FIH rankings, the team's best, followed the league-stage sweep. Malaysia beat Thailand 4-0 and China beat South Korea 1-0 in the other league matches on Wednesday.
stories.whyItMatters: India go into the semifinal against Malaysia unbeaten in the tournament, having rotated fringe players against Japan.

stories.headline: Man United draw 2-2 at Sporting as Lammens error lets in equaliser
stories.dek: Liverpool won 3-0 at Club Brugge in the Champions League, with Alexander Isak scoring twice, after their defeat in the previous round of matches.
stories.summary: Manchester United conceded a late equaliser to Sporting after goalkeeper Senne Lammens spilled a cross, leaving Mauricio Pochettino without a first win. Liverpool beat Club Brugge 3-0, with Alexander Isak scoring twice.
body: Manchester United drew 2-2 with Sporting in Lisbon on Wednesday after goalkeeper Senne Lammens failed to hold a cross, allowing Luis Suarez to score a second goal for the hosts and deny United a Champions League win.
Bruno Fernandes, who used to play for Sporting, scored both United goals. Mauricio Pochettino, who replaced Michael Carrick as coach, is still waiting for his first win in charge.

Suarez missed a first-half penalty after Lisandro Martinez fouled Geny Catamo, with Lammens saving a scuffed effort. A couple of minutes later Lammens left his line and collided with Maxi Araujo, and Suarez scored from the second penalty.

United had an equaliser disallowed before the break. Amad Diallo nodded in a rebound after hitting the crossbar, but Youri Tielemans was ruled to have fouled Goncalo Inacio, although Al Jazeera reported he appeared to win the ball.

Fernandes levelled from the spot early in the second half after Eduardo Quaresma fouled Martinez. He then put United ahead with a low shot from distance that bounced off an uneven patch of turf and over goalkeeper Kaique Pereira.

Sporting equalised when Lammens dropped a cross in front of Suarez, who scored with an acrobatic effort. United then put the ball in the net when Pereira mishandled a Fernandes corner, but the goal was disallowed for an elbow by Patrick Dorgu on the goalkeeper. The visitors were unhappy with that decision as well.
Tielemans was sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card. Fernandes said before the match that he had halted contract talks to focus on improving United's form.

Elsewhere in the competition, Liverpool beat Club Brugge 3-0 away. Alexander Isak scored twice and Florian Wirtz also scored, BBC News reported, as Liverpool recovered from defeat in their previous Champions League match.

Bruno Fernandes scored both United goals; Luis Suarez scored both for Sporting.
Youri Tielemans was sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card.

stories.background: Pochettino took charge of United after Michael Carrick left. His first match was a 4-0 Premier League defeat by Liverpool at the weekend, which left United 19th, according to Al Jazeera.
stories.whyItMatters: United's draw leaves Pochettino without a win in his opening matches, while Liverpool's victory follows their defeat in the previous Champions League round.

stories.headline: South Africa beat Bangladesh by an innings and 219 runs in second Test
stories.dek: Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto said his side lacked capability and consistency after the defeat at Centurion, which followed a nine-wicket loss in Johannesburg.
stories.summary: South Africa won the second Test against Bangladesh at SuperSport Park, Centurion, by an innings and 219 runs on day three. Bangladesh, bowled out for 91 in their first innings, lost the series 2-0.
body: South Africa beat Bangladesh by an innings and 219 runs on the third day of the second Test at SuperSport Park in Centurion on Tuesday, completing a 2-0 series win.

Bangladesh were bowled out for 91 on the first day, which was shortened. According to ESPNcricinfo, they were out of the contest from that point. Their pace bowlers then missed the right lines and lengths in helpful conditions, and their fielders dropped several catches.

South Africa had won the first Test at the Wanderers in Johannesburg by nine wickets. In that match Kagiso Rabada took eight wickets and made a career-best 72, and was named player of the match, according to The Guardian.

Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto did not dispute the result. "There is certainly a lack of capability that must be acknowledged," he said. He added that Bangladesh had played some good cricket at times but needed to do so consistently.

Shanto said the batters had nicked too many balls outside off stump. "As a batting unit, we need to leave those balls if we want to bat long," he said. He finished the series with 61 runs in two Tests. Mominul Haque, Mushfiqur Rahim and newcomer Mahfijul Islam also struggled, according to ESPNcricinfo.
In the second innings Bangladesh built an opening partnership of more than 50. Shanto said batters who were set should have stayed in longer.

Bangladesh have not won an international match in ten attempts since beating Australia in Darwin in August, and have lost their last six Tests, according to ESPNcricinfo. Shanto cited preparation, saying the back-to-back series left too little time. "I'm not making any excuses," he said.
Towhid Hridoy was a bright spot, scoring 137 in the first innings in Johannesburg. Shanto called it a "relief" for a captain to have such a batter at No. 5.

Bangladesh were bowled out for 91 on the truncated first day.

stories.headline: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65 after prostate cancer
stories.dek: The band's former guitarist, who co-wrote hits including Hungry Like the Wolf era songs, died at home surrounded by family, his wife Tracey said.
stories.summary: Andy Taylor, guitarist of Duran Duran during the band's 1980s peak, has died aged 65 after a long illness with prostate cancer. His bandmates and wife Tracey announced the news on Wednesday.
body: Andy Taylor, the guitarist who helped drive Duran Duran's rise in the 1980s, has died aged 65 after a long battle with prostate cancer, his bandmates and family announced on Wednesday.

The band posted the news on its website and Instagram. Billboard reported that the announcement said Taylor died two days earlier. Pitchfork, citing a statement from his wife Tracey to Variety, reported that he died on Monday at home, surrounded by family.

"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor said in a joint statement. "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music." The other band members are not related to him.
Le Bon also issued a personal statement. "There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart," he said.

Tracey Taylor said: "To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather." He is also survived by his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and a grandson, Albie. The couple married in 1982.

Billboard reported that Taylor joined the band in 1980. During his time in the group, Duran Duran had 13 hits on the Billboard Hot 100, including two No. 1s: The Reflex in 1984 and A View to a Kill in 1985. The album Rio, which includes Hungry Like the Wolf, stayed on the Billboard 200 for 128 weeks.

Taylor left in 1985 after the band's Live Aid performance, according to the BBC. In his autobiography, Wild Boy, he described the mood on the bus to the venue as "as if we were on a way to a funeral". He released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.

He rejoined around 2000 or 2001 (the BBC and Billboard give different years) and played on the 2004 album Astronaut before leaving again. He contributed guitar to the 2023 album Danse Macabre, his last work with the band.

His illness became public in 2022, when Duran Duran were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Taylor did not attend, and Le Bon read a letter from him disclosing a diagnosis of stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
The family has asked for privacy.
keyFacts: Andy Taylor died aged 65; the band said he died on Monday.
He had prostate cancer, diagnosed in 2018 according to Pitchfork.
Duran Duran had two Billboard Hot 100 No. 1s during his time in the band.
He is survived by wife Tracey, four children and a grandson.
His last work with the band was the 2023 album Danse Macabre.
stories.background: Duran Duran emerged from Birmingham and became one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, helped by music videos on the newly launched MTV. The band was part of the New Romantic movement. Taylor and bassist John Taylor also formed the side project the Power Station with Robert Palmer in 1984.
